# The Play with No End

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XXIX candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive owner-principal identities. The association of this character with any historical 2016 owner slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. Fara's table house, Eren's shadow play, the hill, its residents, and all dialogue and action here are fictional secondary-world proposals, not reported league history or actual persons' beliefs. This follows Chapter XXVIII: Pell has departed toward an uncertain three-day hauling offer; Ina continues her independent dye trade; Eren's half-paid cart-mark commission is incomplete; the kiln passage remains closed; Jake has received pay for only four stoneworks hours; Mev has accepted Jake's paid letter for an intermediate journey, but Esi's receipt remains unconfirmed. Protected 2026 hard canon remains untouched. Neither editorial approval nor canon promotion is claimed.*

### I. The place where the light stood

The child who had been learning the same high note for three evenings was sitting outside Fara's door with his pipe dismantled on his knees.

He had placed the reed beside him with extraordinary care. A scrap of thread lay across his thumb; with his other hand he was scraping a little dirt from the mouthpiece using the blunt end of a pin. When Jake came along the lower path, the child held the instrument up to the light, inspected it, and put it down again without playing.

"Has it broken?" Jake asked.

"Only when I try the top."

"Then don't try the top."

The child considered this advice as one might consider being told to walk without putting one's feet upon the ground. He returned the reed to its place.

"Do you know how the tune ends?"

"No."

"Neither do they."

He nodded toward the table house. Between its windows a length of linen had been stretched from one upright pole to another. It was not a fine cloth. In daylight it would have shown a dozen repairs, gray seams running across cream-colored ground. Now, with a lamp behind it, the cloth shone orange, and three large dark shapes traveled over its surface without making a sound.

The largest shape had two arms longer than its legs and an enormous head, square at the jaw. Someone moved it closer to the lamp. The head expanded, swallowing half the screen. A smaller figure appeared at one edge, apparently no larger than a spoon, and beat the giant about its knees with a stick. There was a burst of laughter from within.

"What's happening?" Jake asked.

"The show," said the child.

"I can see that."

"Then why did you ask?"

Jake had no answer. He stood beside the boy long enough to hear Fara tell someone inside to stop kicking the table. She sounded less angry than proprietorial: a woman protesting because a piece of furniture knew its own name and would certainly remember the insult.

The boy picked up the pipe. "Eren said I could make the thunder, but thunder isn't the part I know."

"What part do you know?"

"The waiting."

He fitted the reed and played three low notes. The fourth failed with a hard little squeak. From inside came a voice Jake recognized as Eren's.

"That was excellent. Do it again when I say."

"It was wrong," the boy shouted.

"It's meant to be wrong."

He frowned and tried once more, as if determined to prove her mistaken about her own intention.

Fara emerged carrying a bench by one end. She gave Jake the other end without greeting him, and together they carried it beneath the low window. The bench was scarred by countless bowls and elbows. One leg had been set unevenly; it rocked if someone leaned too far toward the wall.

"I thought your room was for suppers," he said.

"It's for whatever people do when they have no other room. Tonight that happens to be frightening each other with socks tied to sticks."

"What are they rehearsing?"

"A thing made up between afternoon and dark. I gave them the linen because nobody was using it, and now apparently a man may not pass through his own doorway without being asked for his opinion of it."

She rubbed her hands on her apron. Her sign hung above them: the painted board Eren had completed and been paid for. The colors looked richer in the lamplight than they had by daylight. The child's pipe made an unhappy fourth note.

"Does Vessa know?" Jake asked.

"Should she?"

He watched the great shadow lean down toward the little one.

"It looks like the warning at the passage."

"Does it?"

"The long arms. The strip across its chest."

Fara squinted at the screen. "I thought it was a tall man carrying two umbrellas."

"There's a watchwoman in it."

"Then there will be a watchwoman in a play," she said, and went inside.

The child followed, pipe first. Jake remained in the yard. He could hear Eren moving the poles, a low tap on the floor when someone dropped a weight, the scrape of a brush being cleaned. A few neighbors came up the lower path. One carried a sleeping infant; another held two cold cakes in a cloth. No one asked Jake why he was there. They simply entered by the door under the painted sign and took places on benches that Fara had not yet finished setting.

He had been told no story about the evening and so had no position from which to object to the story he was about to hear. It was an unfamiliar beginning.

From behind the screen Eren said, "If the tall one falls again, leave it fallen. Don't make everyone run back to put its head on."

There was the soft noise of children laughing into their sleeves.

Jake went inside.

### II. The watchwoman made of kitchen things

A person seeing the puppets from the audience could not tell how they had been made. The long-legged figure looked immense, its face reduced to a cruel angle of nose and chin. But as Jake edged around the rear of the room, he saw the things laid out beside Eren's feet: a crooked ladle, a square of folded paper, two strips of leather, a spoon with its bowl wrapped in dark wool. Nothing bore a likeness until it entered the light.

Four children crouched beneath a rough wooden rail. Eren had painted their hands with a mixture too pale to see well against the linen, so their fingers disappeared when they raised the figures. The boy with the pipe sat near a jar of pebbles and a pot lid. He had been instructed, apparently, to make the sound of a door. In the first attempt he struck the lid so hard that everyone looked at him and the enormous watchwoman fell.

Eren picked up the figure by its stick.

"Again. A door closes because someone shuts it, not because it wants to strike the wall."

"That is what my father's door does," said one of the smaller children.

"Your father's door needs a new hinge."

"It has two."

"Then it needs someone to make them do their work."

She set the puppet upright. Her brush rested in a cup beside her, separate from the half-painted boards for Ina's cart. Those boards had been placed well out of reach of small hands. Jake recognized a bright band of orange near the edge of one. Eren was not neglecting the commission so much as refusing to let her entire evening be owned by it.

"What is the story?" he asked.

"The one they'll tell," she answered.

"About the passage?"

"There's a door in it."

"That isn't what I asked."

"Then listen."

Fara seated the late arrivals. The lamps behind the linen were lowered until only the screen was bright. Eren moved into a darkness Jake could not fully see, and one child struck the pot lid. Another shook the pebbles. The audience quieted, except for the infant who had begun complaining in a dignified, low voice and could not be persuaded that the world required its silence.

The great figure rose in shadow.

"I AM THE KEEPER OF THE HIGH DOOR," said a child with an enormous borrowed voice.

A few adults laughed before anything else occurred. The child waited for quiet, pleased with the power of having interrupted it.

"NONE MAY PASS," announced the keeper. "I HAVE LOCKED THE WIND IN."

The little figure appeared on the opposite side. Its head was a knotted cloth; around its middle was a belt made from a piece of brown string.

"I HAVE A KEY," said a second voice.

"YOU HAVE A SPOON," said the keeper.

"IT IS A KEY WHEN I SAY IT IS."

The audience laughed again. Jake felt an uncomfortable recognition that had nothing to do with the puppet's face. The small figure had been given a short cloak, and beneath it a belt with a conspicuous knot. Its insistence sounded remarkably like him on the road with the freight cart, when he had mistaken the right to speak for a useful command.

The small figure beat at the giant. The keeper fell over. A cluster of tiny shadows poured through the space where she had stood.

"WE ARE FREE," they cried.

The pipe sounded three notes and lost the fourth.

It was a foolish piece of theater, so broad in its effects that even the smallest child understood the joke. The keeper tried to rise and was knocked down again, this time by a wooden spoon so large it obscured the hero. Someone called from the benches that she ought to be allowed a second head. A boy beneath the rail produced one immediately, and for a moment the watchwoman had two dark faces looking in opposite directions.

Jake laughed despite himself.

He stopped when he saw the narrow white strip pinned to the puppet's chest. Eren had copied, not precisely but recognizably, the pale warning fabric Vessa had stretched across the sealed crossing. On a body made of spoons it looked like a decoration for a festival. It made the order to stay back ridiculous.

"The passage wasn't shut for sport," he said, too loudly.

Fara glanced at him from the door.

The child holding the keeper froze. The small hero hung in midair, unable to reach the next blow. People turned. Their faces, half-lit from the audience side, showed different degrees of impatience and curiosity.

Eren did not answer at once. She took the small figure from its stick and handed it to the child beside her. Then she rose and stepped out of the screen's light.

"Nobody said it was," she told Jake.

"The thing they've shown is that someone fought the woman who closed it and made it safe."

"Have they?"

"Look."

Eren looked, obediently, at the frozen shadows. After a while she said, "The boy holding the door has been waiting for you to finish speaking. He has a line."

The boy, finding his courage, declared, "THE KEY IS ALSO A SPOON."

It was, in its way, a difficult line to contradict. The room broke into laughter. Jake stood with his mouth half open, understanding that any further correction would merely make the joke longer.

Eren beckoned the children nearer and gave the hero back its stick. She did not tell Jake he was wrong. That was worse; he could have answered an accusation. Instead she returned to her place behind the linen and asked the boy with the pipe to make the sound of waiting.

The three notes came, low and tentative. On the fourth he did not blow at all.

Behind the screen the watchwoman stood up.

### III. The real woman at the back

The play had reached its second attempt at an ending when Vessa entered.

Jake did not see her cross the threshold. He noticed first that Fara moved a chair aside without speaking, and then that the air near the rear wall had changed. People were no longer watching the screen alone. A woman stood beyond their shoulders in a dusty outer coat, its pale edge marked by the stoneworks yard. She had set down her gloves. Her hands were bare, with a line of dark residue caught beneath the nails.

The watchwoman in the play was threatening to imprison a wind made from scraps of paper. The hero had returned with a painted bird to show it the way through the door.

Vessa watched without expression.

Jake thought of going to her, not to explain the play but to prevent the unkindness he imagined would follow. He had been present when she refused to open the unsafe kiln passage. He knew she had stayed outside with the workers and heard the quarrels about lost hours. He did not know every detail of what the smoke had done behind the closed door. It was enough to understand that the puppet's cruelty was not an observed fact.

But Vessa held up one hand when he moved.

She was listening.

The hero waved the bird. The keeper chased it. The wind blew through. One of the children behind the screen fell sideways with delight and took the keeper down with her. The audience clapped. The story appeared to have finished.

"Again," someone called.

"Let her keep the door this time," said a woman near the window.

"She isn't going to," replied a child.

Eren did not begin again. She stepped out from the side of the linen, a short stick held lightly in her fingers. She had not noticed Vessa, and her eyes moved first to Fara, who tipped her chin toward the rear wall.

The room waited.

"Good evening," Eren said.

Vessa returned the greeting.

"I was going along the lower path," the watchwoman said, "and heard a voice that might have been mine if mine were a roof horn."

A few people laughed. It was neither an accusation nor forgiveness.

"Is it meant to be you?" Fara asked the children.

Three nodded. One shook his head. The boy with the pipe said, "She's taller."

Vessa looked at the puppet whose knees came almost to the top of the screen.

"That must be a difficult woman to feed."

"She doesn't eat," said the youngest girl. "She only says no."

The sentence reached farther than the child could have intended. Jake saw two of the adults lower their gaze. Vessa looked at the girl as she might have looked at a real obstruction in the passage: without contempt, but without the power to step through it.

"I have eaten," she said. "Not particularly well today."

"Then why don't you open the door?"

The question came from the small hero's operator. He had emerged from under the rail, holding the spoon at his side. His voice was no longer borrowed and grand. It was the ordinary voice of a child who had found an adult available to answer him.

Vessa looked toward Jake. He wanted to speak for her and was ashamed of how quickly the words arranged themselves: the smoke, the wrong current, the risk to anyone entering. Those were fragments he had seen, not the whole of her knowledge.

Vessa answered for herself.

"Because it was unsafe when we last checked it."

"But you could check it again."

"We may. Not while you are all standing in Fara's house. Not because a wooden person has opened it."

"That's not fair," the boy said.

"No."

His directness unsettled her less than it unsettled the grown people. She crouched so the spoon and her face were at the same height.

"Did the one who opened your door know what was behind it?"

The boy looked at the screen. "He found a bird."

"Did the bird know?"

"He was the bird."

"Ah," she said.

Eren's face changed. Jake could not tell whether she was pleased or angry that Vessa had found the narrow gap in the story.

"The play isn't a work order," Eren said.

"No," Vessa replied. "And I didn't come with one."

"Then we needn't make it into a hearing."

"I haven't asked you to."

Fara set an empty bowl on the nearest table. The noise of it touching wood was small, yet everyone turned toward her.

"There is room for an audience and room for a guest," she said. "No room for a second passage in my kitchen. If they wish to finish the play, let them. If anyone wishes to eat, I have something left. One of these things can be done without settling the other."

Vessa sat on the chair Fara had moved. The youngest girl asked whether she wanted to hold her own puppet.

"Not tonight," Vessa said.

The girl appeared disappointed. Jake felt a strange tenderness toward her, accompanied by a fear that she might mistake that refusal for the same cruelty as the closed door.

Then Eren asked a question nobody had prepared for.

"How does it end if the door stays shut?"

The children looked at one another. The hero lowered his spoon. Nobody had given them an ending for that version.

### IV. A way around the picture

The children had made the door from a piece of wood no wider than Jake's palm. On the linen it was tall enough to swallow a man. Eren watched them measure the space behind the screen with their hands, stepping from lamp to wall and back again. They were trying to solve a problem in their story as if the problem were a real building: there ought to be a place to stand while the door remained shut, a road for the little people, some occupation for the hero who had brought a key that would not fit.

"We'll knock it down," said the boy with the spoon.

"But she says we can't," said the youngest girl.

"She's not in the story now. She's sitting over there."

Vessa heard and made no objection. She had turned her gloves inside out over her knees, searching for something caught in a seam. The gloves were not theatrical. They belonged to a woman who had been at work, and the audience had begun to look at them with an embarrassment Jake could almost feel in his own hands. The child's figure, meanwhile, had nothing in its possession but a spoon and the confidence of being small.

"Could they dig?" another child asked.

"In the cloth?" Eren said.

"Behind the door."

"Where does behind the door lead?"

"We don't know."

"Then digging might take them somewhere else."

The children conferred. One proposed a tunnel, which required a worm. One proposed that the watchwoman should be asleep, but the girl operating her refused to make her sleep. She had held the stick upright for too long to surrender the large part now. She said the watchwoman should get older and sit down, and everybody might wait until she died.

Fara, who had been pouring soup, stopped with the ladle half raised.

"No one dies in my room merely because a child has run out of words," she said.

"But it would take ages," the child argued.

"Then we'd all be here after the lamps went out. Find a shorter story."

Jake could remember the first time he had stood before the sealed passage and felt the rage of there being no safe gesture he could make. In the play the audience had been allowed a gesture: the spoon struck, the guardian fell, the little people entered. He had laughed with them. Only afterward had the likeness turned cruel.

He wondered whether Vessa had been given such a simple ending at the start of her work. Every decision could be told as if it arose from a single moment in which the door opened or remained shut. But the woman before him had carried her day's failure down the hill with the gloves still on her hands. That was all he knew. He had no right to supply the rest of her thoughts.

Eren put down her brush.

"Suppose the hero can't make the door open," she said. "What does he do that doesn't make him a fool?"

"Then he isn't a hero," said the boy.

"Perhaps not. But he is still there."

The child with the pipe raised a finger. "He could go home."

"And the people?" Eren asked.

"They could go with him."

"Would they all have homes in the same place?"

The child seemed surprised that the question needed asking. Then he looked at the cluster of small figures under the rail. They had been cut from scraps of cloth different in color and thickness, with no likeness between them. He sorted them into two piles. One was larger.

"These ones go," he said. "Those ones stay and wait."

"Why?"

"One has a sore leg."

"Does he have anyone to help him?"

The child searched the remaining shapes and selected one with no arms. He put it beside the lame figure.

"His brother."

It was an answer nobody had prepared. Eren watched the pair for a moment. She did not say that the brother was not strong enough or that no door had been made for them. She took two sticks from the floor and gave them to the child.

"Then show us that."

They began again without announcing a new play. The giant keeper stood with both hands resting against the painted door. The hero raised his spoon. He tapped the wood once, and the hollow sound made the audience shift forward. He tapped a second time. Nothing moved.

"IT IS STILL SHUT," he said.

"IT IS," the watchwoman answered.

In the first version she had bellowed her answer with a voice like a kettle falling down stairs. Now the girl gave her the voice she used when asking for water at supper. The simplicity made her harder to laugh at.

The little figures gathered. Some went left and vanished behind the linen. Some went right, where the lamp could no longer catch them. Two remained at the threshold, one leaning upon the other. The hero tried to lift them both and could not. The boy moved the spoon beneath one of them as a stretcher, but the figure fell off. He tried again, more carefully. Still it fell.

The audience was silent. Even the infant had stopped objecting.

The boy with the pipe played the three low notes. He put his lips to the reed for the fourth, then lowered it. A fourth sound did not come. This time there was no laughter. The light shivered when someone brushed against the lamp's stand.

"Is that the end?" asked a woman at the window.

"No," said the small girl with the keeper.

"Then what happens?"

"I don't know yet."

Jake looked at Fara. She was holding a bowl for a man who had not taken it, and the soup moved gently against the edge while she waited. There was no cruelty in letting the children stop where their story had stopped. Yet he could feel the audience's desire for something completed, a small deliverance they could carry into the cold street.

The boy holding the hero bent low and reached under the rail. He had lost his puppet's left hand. The spoon lay on the boards beside a fallen cloth figure. After some fumbling he reattached the hand with a piece of thread and put the hero upright again.

"WE WILL COME BACK," the small figure said.

The audience began to clap, relieved to have been given a promise.

But the girl holding the keeper struck the rail.

"NO," she cried, suddenly and fiercely.

The clapping ceased.

"You can't say that," she told the boy. "You haven't gone anywhere yet."

For a moment he looked ready to cry. Eren went to the rail, and Jake thought she would intervene on the hero's behalf, as he himself would have tried to do. Instead she took the spoon and set it carefully on the floor, out of both children's reach.

"The next part belongs to another night," she said. "None of us knows it tonight."

The girl still held the great figure upright. The injured pair remained beneath it. The hero, without his spoon, was a piece of knotted cloth tied to a narrow stick. They could have stayed there for an hour, a whole village stopped in shadow.

Then Fara stood and began to collect the bowls.

The action did not end the play. It gave the room permission to return to itself.

### V. The people who could leave

After the lamps were raised, the linen became an ordinary sheet again. A patch near the hem showed through where the weave had worn thin. Fara shook it loose from one pole and folded it across her forearms, waiting while Eren gathered the figures from the floor.

The children were arguing about the next night's version. One still wanted the hero to knock the door down. Another wanted to make a new door that led into a garden. The girl who had held the keeper said there should be no garden until the people who had waited knew what had happened to their friends. Her voice was fierce with the authority of having been made keeper and then discovering that she did not wish to be one forever.

Vessa rose from her chair. The gloves were back on her hands.

"Did I make you angry?" the girl asked her.

"A little," Vessa said.

The girl's face fell. Vessa crouched again, more slowly this time.

"You made something I recognized," she said. "It isn't the same as what happened."

"Then we'll make it like what happened."

"You don't know all of it."

"Tell us."

Vessa rubbed a thumb against a stitch in the glove. Jake could see the silence working on her. He expected a lecture about smoke and dangerous passages, a description of labor that would give the adults a reason to praise the woman's restraint. But she did not explain the world to the children so that they might repeat it correctly.

"Ask me another day," she said. "When I can show you the place you are asking about from where it is safe to stand. I won't open it for your play, and you needn't make your play into my answer."

The child understood the refusal before the offer. She watched Vessa go toward the door, then turned back to the rail where her giant lay. The puppet had lost one of its long arms; a leather strip dangled from its shoulder. With serious concentration she began tying it back on.

Jake followed Vessa into the yard. He had intended to apologize for the scene in Fara's house. By the time he reached her she was already looking up at the real sign above the door.

"Eren did that," she said.

"She was paid for it."

"It looks well."

"Yes."

"She has more patience with a brush than some of us have with people."

It was spoken without bitterness. Jake wanted to tell her that the children's keeper had not truly been a judgment on her, that theater was often unfair and that no one who mattered had believed it. He could not offer the last statement. He had watched men in the audience laugh when the puppet fell, and he had laughed too.

"I should have said something earlier," he began.

"You did."

"Not the right thing."

Vessa looked toward the room. Through the window Jake could see Eren counting pebbles back into the jar. Fara was carrying dishes away. The pipe player had his instrument apart again and was trying to free a knot in the thread with his teeth.

"I don't need you to tell me I was brave," Vessa said. "I don't know yet whether I made every choice I ought to have made. I know the passage was unsafe. The rest of it won't be decided by a spoon."

"I know."

"Then we have nothing more to settle tonight."

She went along the lower path, passing beneath the sign without looking back. Jake heard her steps grow softer against the packed ground. He did not follow.

When he returned inside, the young girl approached him with the hero puppet. Without the lamp behind it the figure was pitifully small: a scrap of cloth for a head, a narrow trunk, a bit of string for a belt. The knot was poorly tied. She held it toward him.

"Can you do what he did?"

"What did he do?"

"Make them laugh."

"I don't think so."

She considered him with the directness he had already begun to dread. "You could be the keeper."

He smiled. "I wouldn't know how."

"You just stand still."

From the rear of the room Eren said, "Don't give away my actors. I'll have none left."

The girl ran back to the rail with her puppet. Jake did not ask whether the hero had been meant to resemble him. It was enough that someone had taken a few pieces of cloth and made a figure people saw from a distance. A person was not required to consent to every likeness in the world. He was also not required to mistake the likeness for proof.

Eren placed Ina's partly painted cart boards flat on a shelf and covered them against dust. The half-paid commission remained work to be completed, not a prop in the evening's story. She was not packing away a dream of being an artist; she had brought her tools to the table house, practiced her craft, and chosen what the children would be permitted to do with it. No one had asked Jake to judge whether this was sufficient for her.

"Will you make another one?" he asked.

"Maybe."

"The keeper ought to have a face."

"She has one. It looks different depending on where the lamp stands."

"Is that on purpose?"

"Most things look different depending on where the lamp stands," Eren replied. "You can help move the poles if you're still here."

He helped. They carried the rail to the dry wall and stood it against the hooks Fara had provided. A peg slipped loose and fell, striking the boards with a sharp crack. The child with the pipe startled and blew the wrong note. Everyone laughed, including him. The sound had escaped by accident, not by finding the ending of the tune.

Fara extinguished the lamp behind the linen last. She checked the bench leg with her foot, moved the jar of crooked nails away from a child's reach, and told the late guests that the room would be open for supper on the following evening whether there was a show or not. She made no promise about the play.

Outside, the path toward the stoneworks was dark enough that Jake had to feel the edge of the step with his boot. The warning strip across the sealed passage remained where Vessa had placed it. Pell had gone toward an uncertain three-day hauling offer; Ina's orders would still travel whether he returned or not. Eren's cart marks would be finished when Eren finished them. The four hours Jake had actually been paid for remained the only new stoneworks wages in his bag. Mev might carry his letter onward, or might have handed it to someone else on the intermediate route; no word had come back from Esi. None of these things had been transformed by a night of children making giants from kitchen utensils.

Yet a room had become a different kind of room while he sat within it. The inhabitants of the hill had made an account of their own disappointment, and then declined to improve it for his comfort. Vessa had walked out with the real gloves on her hands. The children had put the false hero away without destroying him. Even Fara's house had a life Jake could only enter when invited.

The pipe sounded once more through the window. Three notes and a silence. He waited for the fourth. It did not come.

Behind him a small voice called, "We don't know that part yet."

He was far enough along the path that he could not tell whether the words were addressed to him or to someone inside. He kept walking without answering.

---

# The Fourth Note at the River

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XXX candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive owner-principal identities. His binding to any historical 2016 scoring slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. Fara's table house, the stoneworks settlement, Tavin and his family, the old ferry landing, river weather, local crafts and all actions and dialogue are proposed secondary-world fiction, not league history, actual owner testimony, or approved Atlas/period canon. The preceding chapter left a children's shadow play intentionally unfinished; Vessa's dangerous kiln passage remains closed; Eren's half-paid cart-mark commission is incomplete; Pell's three-day hauling engagement and wages are unconfirmed; Mev holds Jake's outward letter for an unverified intermediate delivery to Esi; Jake's only newly earned stoneworks wages remain four paid hours, and his shelter debts are not discharged. No historical result or real-world private motive is invented.*

### I. A reed in the wrong place

The morning after the play, there was a pipe reed on the ledge of Fara's eastern window.

It had been set upon a clean square of cloth, though the cloth itself was old and one corner was scorched. A stone no larger than a plum held the edge down against the wind. Jake might have passed it without noticing had Fara not come out of the house with two empty bowls and stopped so suddenly that the bowls knocked together.

"That wasn't there when I opened."

She put the bowls beneath her arm and took up the reed by its uncut end. The little piece of cane had a dark line where a mouth had worn it smooth. Jake remembered the boy outside her door, scraping dirt from the mouthpiece with a pin and asking how a tune ended.

"Perhaps he left it for you."

"Perhaps he lost it. Those are different troubles."

She looked toward the lower path, which still held the pale dust of yesterday's feet. Nobody was walking there. The table-house sign swung once on its iron loops and settled.

"What's his name?" Jake asked.

"Tavin. You heard him all evening."

"I heard a pipe."

"You heard Tavin. There's a difference in that, too."

Fara carried the reed inside. The room looked smaller in daylight. The linen screen was gone; beneath the hooks on the wall the rail lay on its side, showing the knots that had held it upright. There was no giant keeper now, no little hero with a string belt. There were stools badly stacked, a chipped cup, a heap of pebbles and a brass pot lid that seemed almost embarrassed to be an instrument. Eren's paints were arranged along the far shelf. The two boards for Ina's cart lay face down on a piece of sacking, safe from dust but still unfinished.

Fara placed the reed where the children had stood.

"His father was supposed to collect him after the show."

"Did he?"

"Someone did. I didn't stand at the door counting fathers." She picked up the cup. "They stayed long enough to help set the benches back. I went to sleep believing everybody had gone home."

A bell sounded from the stoneworks yard: not a summons to open the dangerous passage, but the ordinary short signal that marked the start of a permitted shift outside it. Jake had been told there would be no work for him that morning. He had already come down to the table house because the room had been full of voices yesterday and the silence in his lodging had seemed larger for it.

A little girl came through the door with a roll of linen under one arm. She had held the puppet of the great watchwoman.

"Where's Tavin?" Fara asked.

The girl looked toward the shelf. "He said he wasn't doing the thunder again."

"That's not what I asked."

"He took the pipe apart."

"Where is he now?"

"He said the fourth one wasn't in the house."

Fara stood very still. The girl seemed surprised that her answer had troubled anybody. She unrolled the linen. It was the same repaired sheet they had used for the screen. The gray seams ran across it like roads that had been built without agreeing where to meet.

"Was he going to fetch it?" Jake asked.

"He said he knew where to listen."

"Where?"

"Outside."

The answer was not insolence. It was all she knew.

Fara went to the doorway and called along the path, not yet loudly. A man at the nearby well lifted his hand to indicate that he had heard, but he did not come over. When no answer arrived from the bend below, Fara asked the girl to go home and tell Tavin's father exactly what she had said. She told her not to look for Tavin alone.

"I can run very fast."

"I know. Run home."

The girl went. Fara set down the cup, and Jake saw that the bottom was cracked almost through. She had been carrying it without looking at it, as people carry things when their hands are occupied with a thought.

"Maybe he's in his bed," he said.

"Maybe."

She did not thank him for the possibility. She took the reed again, held it for a moment beneath the window, then folded it into her palm.

"Find Eren. She knew what he was making."

Jake went into the morning.

### II. The search people wanted to make

Eren was kneeling beside Ina's cart, putting the first coat of a dark line around one of the promised marks. The vehicle stood in a yard that smelled of wet bark and boiled roots, though the nearest dye pot was cold. Ina held a strip of cloth against the wheel so that Eren could judge the distance from the rim.

"No, lower," Ina said.

"If I put it lower, the iron will take half the paint."

"Then I asked for the wrong place."

"You asked for a mark that would survive the road. This is where it can live."

Eren drew the line without looking up. She had threaded a cord through the spoke to keep the wheel from moving, and the end of the cord lay near her heel. Her small knife, brush and rag were arranged in a deliberate row. Whatever happened elsewhere in the settlement, the commission was real work. Ina had given her the first half of the payment, and the balance remained due only upon the completed pair of boards.

Jake waited until Eren lifted the brush.

"Tavin's gone missing."

She looked at him then. "Missing from where?"

"Fara found his reed. He told one of the girls the fourth note wasn't in the house."

Eren touched the brush to the rag. "He told me something like that after the show."

"Did he say where it was?"

"He asked whether a sound can stay in a place after the person who made it has gone."

Ina let the cloth fall away from the wheel. Neither woman spoke for a moment. A small breeze shifted the loose edge of the cart cover.

"What did you tell him?" Jake asked.

"That a place may help you remember, but it can't sing in your stead."

"You didn't ask what he meant?"

"I thought he was talking about his pipe." Eren set the brush down. "I was talking about paint and lamps and who had taken the lid home. I ought to have listened longer."

Ina bent and loosened the cord from the wheel. "Go if you need to," she told Eren. "The boards can remain boards for another hour."

"I'll come back."

"Come back because you mean to finish them, not because I have caught you leaving."

Eren wiped her fingers and rose. The paint had left a crescent beneath one nail. She seemed about to say something to Ina, but instead she took a strip of clean cloth from her roll and wrapped it around the brush so the bristles would not harden.

At the kiln passage, two men were already pulling on the locked outer gate.

Tavin's father, Harl, was one of them. Jake knew him by sight: a broad-shouldered worker whose right ear bent slightly away from his head. The other man had a short iron lever wedged into a seam. He was not trying to be destructive, or not only destructive. He had the fixed expression of someone determined that a barrier must become an answer.

"We heard a pipe near this wall," Harl said when Vessa came out from the yard.

"When?"

"At first light. I thought he was with the children. Then Fara sent for me."

Vessa put her hand on the lever but did not wrench it away. "The outer gate remains closed."

"He's small enough to slip through."

"There is nowhere to slip through from that side without moving this gate."

"Then move it."

"Not before we know he's there."

The other man cursed. "You'll let a boy stay inside because you need a certificate to use your own hands?"

"I will not take down a barrier to send four men into a passage we have not made safe," she said. "You can search the drainage edge, the outside sheds and the river track. I'll send two people who know those places. If there's evidence he went under this gate, we change the search. No one has shown me that yet."

Harl stepped closer. "He's my son."

"I know."

"Do you?"

Vessa's mouth tightened. Jake stood beside Eren, wanting to offer a third answer that would bring relief without risk. He could find none. He had seen the closed passage, and he had seen the enormous false keeper fall before a spoon. He had not gone behind the gate. The difference seemed cruelly thin.

Eren showed Harl the reed Fara had entrusted to her. The man took it and looked at the worn dark line.

"He took the old one," he said.

"Old?"

"This is what his mother cut for him. He made another last summer and that one hardly speaks at all."

"Did she teach him the tune?" Eren asked.

"Three notes." He closed his hand around the reed. "She was ill by then. I told him the rest was easy. That wasn't a thing I knew."

He turned toward the gate again, but the other man had already withdrawn the lever. Vessa was calling workers to the permitted paths. The search had become something that could be done, not a choice between breaking the gate and doing nothing.

Jake followed Eren toward the old river track. Harl stayed long enough to tell Vessa which bend his son had once gone to with his mother. When he came after them, his steps were quick and uneven, and he did not ask anybody to wait.

### III. Where the bank held the sound

The path to the former ferry landing passed under willows whose low branches held the night rain. Between them the river showed itself in narrow pieces of dull silver. Jake had been along the working ferry road before, with goods to carry and a wage to earn. This was a different track. Its stones had sunk into the ground, and roots curled around them as if the path were a thing the trees had decided to keep.

Eren led because she knew where the children went when adults were busy. The rail from the play would never have reached here; the lamps would have gone out before the screen was carried half the way. Yet the place was close enough that a child could cross it in a single morning, especially one who did not know his absence had become an emergency.

They found the first sign beside a shallow pool. A small shoeprint had filled with water in a stretch of smooth mud. Beside it were two larger prints and the marks of a narrow wheel. They could have belonged to almost anyone. Jake crouched anyway, grateful to have something he could look at without choosing what it meant.

"Don't go down there," Eren said.

He looked up. Beyond the pool the bank dropped sharply to a tongue of gravel. Water passed the gravel on both sides. At low river it might have been a place to stand and hear the sound rise between the stone walls. Now the gravel was slick, and the outer edge had disappeared beneath a slow brown curl.

"There's a way farther back," she said. "It comes out above the landing."

They went around.

Above the old steps stood a low stone shelter with half its roof gone. The surviving roof beams were black with weather, not fire. Someone had hung fishing line from a peg and neglected to retrieve it. The landing itself was no longer a place where boats regularly called; upriver, the working ferry remained the reliable crossing. Here the water moved as if the river remembered the old traffic but had ceased to wait for it.

Eren called Tavin's name. The only answer was the small, repetitive knocking of an unsecured board against stone.

Harl called too, and Jake heard the fear turn his voice unrecognizable. The man tried to descend the wet steps, but Eren caught his sleeve.

"Listen first."

"I'm listening."

"No. Listen."

She took the reed from his fist, held it between her fingers and blew, without its pipe, the faintest possible breath across it. The sound was scarcely musical: a reed of air, an insect's complaint. It disappeared under the river's noise. She tried again.

From beneath the ruined roof came a low answering note.

Harl moved at once. Eren reached past him and held up a hand; not because she had an authority there, but because the sound had come from somewhere he was not looking.

"Tavin," she called, "we're above you."

There was a pause. Then a child's voice said, "You shouldn't come down the wet way."

Jake stepped to the broken wall. Below the shelter, a dry shelf ran behind a row of stones. Tavin sat there with his knees drawn up, a small pipe lying beside his shoe. He had not gone through the dangerous kiln gate. He had not crossed the river. He had found a place where the wall threw sound back at its maker, and now the water had risen enough to cover the lowest steps he had used.

"Can you come up the high way?" Eren asked.

"I came the low way."

"I know. Can you see a row of stone notches behind you?"

"Yes."

"Those are steps. Follow them until you reach the post."

"I don't want to."

Harl leaned forward. "Get up here."

"Not that way."

"What do you mean, not that way?"

The boy put a hand on the little pipe, although he did not pick it up. Jake could see his fingers trembling. His trousers were wet almost to the knees. He might have been cold; he might have been afraid of the scolding awaiting him. Jake could not tell.

Eren sat on a sound part of the upper wall, lowering herself until she was no taller than the boy appeared below.

"You came to listen for the rest of the tune," she said.

"No."

"What did you come for?"

"I thought it would be here if I was quiet."

"What would?"

"The part she hadn't finished."

Harl made a sound unlike a word. He withdrew from the edge and stood with his hands on his hips, facing the willows. Jake could see the man's shoulder moving beneath his coat.

Tavin spoke to Eren, not to his father.

"When I was little she used to make the echo. I thought it was another person. She said that was how you knew a place was listening. Then she couldn't come anymore."

The river struck the old steps. Beneath the shelter the loose board knocked twice against its stone. Tavin looked at the pipe.

"If I go home, nobody can tell me the rest."

There was enough truth in the statement to frighten Jake. He remembered arriving at the shelter after his first journey from the stoneworks and wanting his return to restore the place he had left. The shelter had changed; the missing bed had not been waiting in its old position. He had resented the new inhabitant for occupying a life that had continued without him. He knew now how strange it was to want a place to keep a person's unfinished business intact.

Eren answered before he could make that memory into advice.

"Then we won't pretend it has been waiting for you," she said. "You can come up without deciding what the fourth note is."

Tavin stared at the high steps. "Father will make me finish it."

Harl turned around. His face looked older in the gray light than it had at the kiln wall.

"I told you the rest was easy," he said. "I was wrong."

The boy watched him as if listening for a trap.

"I don't know the note," Harl said. "I can't make it hers. I never could."

He did not step down to carry Tavin. Instead he moved to the upper end of the notched stones, where the shelf would bring the boy within reach. Vessa's searchers appeared on the path behind them, called by the voices. One of them brought a length of rope and held it ready but unused. The boy rose, testing each stone with the flat of his shoe before putting weight on it. He kept a hand against the wall.

At the fourth step he stopped.

"I left the pipe."

"Leave it," Harl said.

Tavin sat down at once. Eren did not tell him the object was unimportant. She went to the end of the upper wall, found a dry crack where she could climb a short way down without entering the water, and reached the pipe with the long end of a fallen branch. It caught under the cord, slid, almost fell, then came toward her in a slow scrape. She passed it up to Jake, who stood where he had been asked to stand and took it without ceremony.

Only then did the boy climb the rest of the way.

Harl knelt. He opened his arms but did not pull his son into them. Tavin walked the last step by himself and stood for a moment as if unsure of the distance between two bodies. Then he pressed his face into his father's shoulder. The man held him until the boy's shaking passed. No one cheered. One of the searchers turned away to look at the water; another wound the unused rope around his elbow.

The old landing continued to make its soft, empty noise.

### IV. A room that could no longer be innocent

When they returned to Fara's house, the other children were waiting outside.

The girl who had held the watchwoman ran toward Tavin and stopped a few paces away. She had been brave enough to play a monster before the whole room, but now she seemed unable to decide whether to embrace him or strike him.

"You said you were going to listen," she said.

"I did."

"You didn't say we'd have to look."

Tavin took the pipe from Jake without meeting her eyes.

Harl began to explain where the boy had gone. Fara stopped him with a touch on his sleeve and drew him inside, where there were stools and water and a place to hear a father's account without setting it before the children as a performance. Vessa had come from the kiln track. She told the searchers to return to their assignments and checked that the unsafe outer gate had not been moved. The closure remained in force.

For a short while the room filled with stories that were already changing. A man said Tavin had been beneath the kiln; another said he had crossed the river and been found on the farther bank; a woman who had not joined the search said the boy had heard the music of his dead mother and followed it into a cave. Each story made the search longer, more perilous, more satisfying to retell.

Eren set her knife on the table. Its small noise stopped the nearest speakers.

"He was on the dry shelf below the old landing," she said. "The steps were wet. He walked out by the high way. No one opened the kiln passage, and no one went into the river."

The woman with the cave story objected, "That is what I heard."

"Then you heard it badly."

Jake had an impulse to add details: the shoeprints, the branch, the sound of the loose board. He held back. His memory was already preparing itself for an account in which he had understood the danger from the beginning. He had not. He had looked at mud and thought it must mean something. Eren had known where to listen. Vessa had kept the right barrier shut. Harl had told the truth his son needed, late as it was. Jake had held a recovered pipe, a modest weight.

Harl came out after giving Tavin dry stockings. He looked from the screen hooks to the pot lid beside the shelf.

"Was it the play?" he asked Eren.

"I don't know."

"He played that tune because you put him behind a sheet for people to laugh at."

"He was learning it before I borrowed the sheet."

"Then you ought to have asked why he couldn't finish."

Eren looked at Tavin, who was drinking water from a bowl at Fara's table. The boy had been given a piece of bread and had eaten half, leaving the other half untouched.

"I ought to have listened longer," she said.

Harl seemed unsettled by the admission. It left him with anger that could not find a single person to hold. "If you put that thing up again," he said, gesturing toward the hooks, "I won't have him in it."

"That's your choice to make with him."

"It's mine."

"And his," Fara said from the doorway.

The man's jaw tightened. Fara did not raise her voice. She drew a stool out for him but did not compel him to sit.

"A room doesn't make a child safe merely because adults are in it," she said. "Nor does it make him unsafe because he played a fool's tune. We have to know where the children are when they leave, and we have to notice when they have something they cannot tell us at supper."

"You weren't counting fathers yesterday."

"No," Fara said. "I wasn't."

They allowed that answer to stand. It was neither pardon nor accusation, and for once no one found an advantage in improving it.

The girl with the watchwoman puppet pulled the broken leather arm out from under the shelf. She held it as one might hold a dead bird.

"Are we never doing the play again?"

No one answered at once. Eren stood by the window, looking at the linen folded on the sill. Jake expected her to declare that art must remain free, as she had done in smaller ways throughout the previous night. Instead she took down the hanging cord and began winding it around the wooden rail.

"We won't do that play tonight," she said.

The girl frowned. "Because of Tavin?"

"Because I don't know what we're making next. And because I said we'd ask who wanted to be in it."

"You didn't ask before."

"I know."

"Does that mean it was wrong?"

"It means we can do the next thing differently."

Tavin lifted his eyes from his bread. "I want to play," he said quietly.

Harl looked at him. "You don't have to."

"I know."

"What would you play?"

"Not the keeper."

The boy turned the pipe in his hand, making the worn reed catch the morning light.

"I could play the river," he said.

Eren smiled, but only a little. "Then you'd better listen to it first, in a place someone knows you're going."

The girl put the puppet arm on the shelf. A new argument began immediately about whether a river should have a mouth or only hands. The children were disagreeing like children again, with no regard for the elegance of the lesson adults might have wished to draw from them.

Ina came through the open door carrying the two cart boards under her arm.

"I found your work covered," she told Eren. "I kept it out of the rain. Will you finish it here or at my yard?"

Eren looked down at her paint-stained hands. "At your yard. The wheel is there."

"Good. I'll bring fresh water for the brushes."

She left the boards where Eren could take them when she was ready. Their dark outlines had dried without splitting. The commission had not been completed, and the second half of the payment had not been earned. Neither woman called it lost.

The room smelled of bread and damp wool. Outside, the river kept moving beyond the visible houses, too far away to hear. The sheet, folded, was only cloth. Fara went to the shelves and began the work of preparing the midday meal.

### V. Not the same song

Jake returned to the old landing before sunset, though he did not go down the wet steps.

A little above the ruined roof he found a place where the river could be seen in two directions. Upstream the water narrowed between pale rocks; downstream it spread into a broader bend under alder branches. A working boat passed in the distance, its oars moving at a pace too steady to belong to rescue. The river had kept the same course since morning without becoming innocent of what had nearly happened upon its edge.

He had brought nothing to leave there. He stood with his hands empty.

It was a poor place for a monument, he thought, because every sound was taken apart almost as soon as it appeared. A voice called from the other bank and returned as an indistinct beat. The former ferry shelter answered the wind with its loose board. Water touched the stones in irregular pairs. He could hear how a child might believe that some other person was trying to complete a tune.

He had wanted to tell Harl that his son was brave. He had wanted to tell Tavin that grief could be carried without being finished. He had wanted to tell Eren that a play could make room for what a community would not say at supper. They would have been handsome things to say. They would not have been the things any of them had asked him to know.

On the return path he passed Vessa near the closed passage. She was taking down a notice whose ink had blurred in the damp and putting up another with larger marks. She had not reopened the gate. A worker held the ladder for her. Neither of them asked Jake for an opinion. When she descended, she looked at his empty hands.

"Was he there?" she asked.

"At the landing. He's home now."

"I know that. I meant the place you were looking for."

Jake considered answering that there was nothing left to find. The reed, the wet steps, the father kneeling, the unspoken fourth note were all still there in the kind of memory that did not need a witness. Yet he had not been looking for evidence, or a missing child. He had gone because the landing was a place other people had used before he knew it, and would go on using or abandoning without his permission.

"I think so," he said.

"Then come away from the gate. We'll need clear ground here in the morning."

He moved. The gate remained shut behind her.

At Fara's house a lamp had been lit early. Through the window he saw Ina seated with a bowl of soup, her unfinished blue coat folded on the bench beside her. There was no word that Pell's uncertain hauling offer had become paid work or that he had returned from it. Ina ate without making her waiting a public matter.

Eren was washing the last brush in a shallow cup. Both cart boards lay on the table, their marks completed to the edges and drying in a line of warm air above the hearth. Jake could not tell whether Ina had accepted them or settled the remaining payment, and did not ask. The actual completion of the painted work was visible enough. Fara was counting spoons, finding one too many and setting it aside.

Tavin sat by the eastern window. The pipe rested against his knee.

Harl had joined him but was not watching his fingers. They were looking toward the path, where the last light caught on the stones. The boy put the reed into place, wetted it, and began to play. The first three notes were the ones Jake knew: low, lower, then a rising uncertainty. He waited for the familiar broken squeak.

A fourth note came.

It was not high. It did not conclude the phrase. It turned the tune away from the direction Jake had expected, leaving a space afterward so wide that for a moment he thought the child had simply stopped.

Harl looked at him.

"That's not how she played it," he said.

"No," Tavin answered.

The man nodded. He did not correct his son.

The pipe began again, this time with the fourth note already belonging to the tune. Tavin missed it once and tried again. The room did not fall silent for him; Fara continued setting the table, Eren tipped out dirty brush water, and someone beyond the door laughed at a joke Jake could not hear. The melody was part of their evening now, not the price of it.

Jake stood outside until the child reached the new note a third time. Then he opened the door and went in to supper.

He had earned no more money that day. He had received no proof that Mev's letter reached Esi. No river expedition had identified the thief of the shelter ledger; no word had come that Mara and Senn were safe in their uncertain weaving journey, nor that Sola's privacy work had settled the harm done to her. Vessa's kiln remained shut, Pell's hauling remained unconfirmed, and the work waiting for tomorrow had not been made easier by a tune.

But Eren's boards were drying. Tavin had chosen a note that was not his mother's. Harl had heard the difference and allowed it to exist. In Fara's house, the people who had searched all day were eating with the people who had waited for news; nobody was being asked to call the search a victory.

The boy played four notes again. His father asked for the pipe, attempted the same phrase, and made a sound so astonishingly unlike music that Tavin laughed with his whole body. It startled everyone at the table. Harl laughed too, holding up the instrument as though it were a small but formidable wild animal.

Eren reached for her dry boards. Ina touched one lightly with a finger and drew it back when the paint marked her skin. They began speaking in the ordinary, precise language of a customer and the maker of something meant to withstand a road. Fara brought the last loaf. Vessa, passing in the dark beyond the window, did not stop.

Jake took a place at the end of the bench where no one had reserved a seat for him. He listened while the tune began again, hearing the silence after the new note not as a failure to finish, but as the part in which another voice might one day enter.
