# The Feast with No Vows

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XXXIII candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive owner-principal identities. His identification with any historical 2016 league scoring slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. All people other than the proposed fictional Jake, personal and household relationships, wedding customs, food, architecture, geography, decisions, institutions, dialogue and material events here are secondary-world invention for editorial consideration; none is an asserted real ESPN/Flaim result, actual biography, approved period Atlas or Character Canon. Entering state: Ina and Eren returned safely, Eren's separate map and cart-fitting work paid, Ina dye business active; Pell, the driver, second horse and freight missing and an unidentified empty cart awaiting properly equipped carrier inquiry; injured mare receiving bounded stable care; Fara's dining room restored; kiln passage still closed, Jake's older shelter debts unpaid, two earlier bounded stoneworks wages earned but no later rain-day wages, and Mev's delivery of his message to Esi unconfirmed. No new 2016 competition facts are introduced.*

### I. The table measured twice

They had built the wedding table in a place too narrow to hold it.

Jake could see the mistake before he saw the wedding. The long boards had been set on trestles between the stone wall of a little courtyard and a row of pear trees trained against its opposite side. There was room for people to sit, if they came through the gate one at a time and kept their knees under the boards. There would be no room for anybody carrying a bowl, and the serving women would have to pass their pots across the backs of the guests.

Noll stood at the far end with a measuring cord in his hand. He had the expression of a man trying to persuade a length of timber to become shorter by addressing it firmly.

“It's the right size,” he called to Jake. “The yard is the wrong size.”

“You measured the yard?”

“Twice.”

“Before they set up the table?”

“After the first attempt. I wasn't going to repeat the mistake.”

Fara, arriving with her hired hand and two covered baskets, stopped at the gate and regarded the narrow passage. Her room had been restored after the days of the injured mare and anxious strangers, and she was not inclined to lose another afternoon to someone else's enthusiasm. The food in her baskets was paid for. She had made a simple arrangement with the two households: bread, a pot of onions with beans, two dishes of dried fruit, and enough bowls to serve those invited. Whatever the families wished to promise one another was their business. Whatever they wished to add to the meal would have to fit on the table.

“Move it,” she told Noll.

“The bride's uncle told me not to move it after he laid out the cloth.”

“Then he may serve the food through the wall.”

Noll scratched his chin. He looked toward Jake, who held his arms at his sides rather than volunteering to lift the trestle.

“Perhaps we could carry it outside the gate,” Noll said.

“Then there's no point in having a courtyard.”

“You could cut the end off,” Jake said.

“No one is cutting the wedding table,” a woman answered from behind him.

She was older than either of the people who were to make the vows, and her jacket was made of a dark material polished by long use at the elbows. She carried a needle between her lips. Without looking at the men again she removed it, set a stitch in the edge of the cloth, and drew the thread tight.

“I am Serra,” she said. “Lysa's aunt. I made the cloth. The table fits.”

Fara lifted her baskets. “The cloth may fit. The people must eat.”

Serra inspected the gap between the wall and the nearest board. She moved a stool with her foot, placed it beyond the gate, and said, “The younger ones can stand.”

“Then they're not sitting at a wedding table,” Noll said.

“They can stand at a wedding table.”

The discussion might have continued until the guests arrived. Instead a boy carrying a pail came through the courtyard, tried to squeeze behind Noll, and tipped a little water onto the paving. Everyone moved to avoid the wet patch, and for an instant the narrow space looked like a passage full of people attempting to evade one another rather than a place where two households could meet.

Jake took the near end of the table when Fara asked him. Noll took the far end. They lifted together, rotated the boards a quarter turn, and set them against the pear wall, where the serving side was open and the cloth still lay flat. The bride's uncle, summoned too late to prevent the change, protested that the head of the table now faced the wrong direction. Fara replied that the beans would not know which way they faced.

The uncle stared at her. He had been introduced as Daro, though Jake was unsure whether that was his name or the name the younger men used to avoid addressing him properly. He wore a pale sash and carried a round wooden object with two holes, which he said was the token of the two houses. He set it on the table, as if that would settle orientation.

Noll took up the measuring cord again. This time he measured the walking space. It was sufficient. The bride's uncle was displeased but did not move the boards back.

Jake had not been asked to serve as a witness. He was there because Noll needed hands, and because the stoneworks keeper had again offered no new outside sorting shift that morning. Jake had earned money on earlier days and still had a little of it; he had not earned more by walking up the hill and being sent away. He could carry a table without believing it would repair his fortunes. The older shelter debt remained in its own place, where no courtyard work could reach it.

The two families had gathered for Lysa and Corin, both grown and present in the settlement for several seasons, though Jake had met neither of them. Noll said their households had quarreled over a drying shed and then made peace enough to share the cost of a new roof. The wedding was supposed to make the peace visible. Jake did not know whether either of the people being married had asked to become its proof.

The bride did not appear while they arranged the bowls. The groom, Corin, came into the courtyard carrying a bundle of young branches to hang above the gate. He set them down beside Serra and asked where the knife had gone. His hands were clean and the skin beneath his fingernails pale. He was dressed more carefully than anyone had dressed to carry food in the wet streets that week.

“Do you like it?” Noll asked him, indicating the table.

Corin looked at the rotated boards, the cloth still even across them, and the path open for serving. “People can get through.”

“That's not an answer,” Noll said.

“It's the answer I've got.”

Serra gave the groom a measuring glance. “You should be waiting inside. It isn't proper to be carrying the arch.”

“Someone had to carry it.”

“Someone else could have.”

Corin bent to retrieve the fallen branches. He did not quarrel with her. Jake watched him place them along the gateposts with a care that was almost severe, tying each with the narrow ends turned inward. They looked fine once they were up. The courtyard acquired the appearance of a place ready for something important, though nobody had yet said who would make it happen.

Fara passed among the trestles and began to set out her food. At one end of the yard, somebody was practicing three notes on a small pipe, uncertainly enough that no one could mistake the noise for a command. The guests began arriving. There was no sign of Lysa.

### II. A ceremony of borrowed words

The guests wore small signs of belonging that Jake did not know how to read.

One household had tied narrow strips of green cloth around the wrist; the other had pinned yellow flowers to the collar. Some wore both. A woman who had been asked to prepare the bread came with flour on her sleeve and a strip of each color, and a boy accused her of taking sides against herself. She answered that she was on the side of eating.

Fara gave the boy a bowl to carry and instructed him not to swing it by the rim. He walked with exaggerated dignity until he set it down. A man at the gate called him a fine servant. The boy's face changed at once. He had been glad to help before anyone named what that made him.

Noll set a stool for the old woman who had arrived with two sticks and a shallow basket of dates. She refused it because it faced the wrong way. He turned it toward the gate. She refused again because the sun would strike her eyes. He moved it into the shade by the pear tree and she sat without thanking him. Her small victories were apparently a part of the ceremony.

Corin passed from group to group, greeting people he knew by name. He asked several whether they had come a long distance, though the settlement was small enough that Jake expected most had walked. When an elderly man embraced him, the groom stood quite still until the man let him go. He spoke readily with the older women, less readily with the men in pale sashes. Several guests offered him advice on how to behave toward his future household. Their sayings contradicted one another. He received each as though it had been the first.

“Do they tell the bride as much?” Jake asked Noll.

“More. But they speak to her through the aunt.”

“Why?”

“Serra likes being heard.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“No,” Noll said. “It rarely is.”

Noll had known Corin's father when the two had carried timber for a roof belonging to neither household. The family quarrel, he explained, had begun over use of a drying shed at the edge of the courtyard, and in the end the repair had been paid by people on both sides. The shed stood now on a shared plot with a new roof and no agreement that made everybody happy. Jake had seen enough of borrowed buildings to understand how a roof could remain solid while the relationships beneath it failed.

“Was the wedding meant to settle who uses the shed?” he asked.

“Some people say it makes the argument family business.”

“Isn't it already family business?”

“That's why they want it settled.”

Noll's answer amused him less the longer he considered it. He wanted to know what Lysa had said. Noll could tell him only what other people said she had said. That ought to have ended the question, but Jake listened anyway when Noll described the elaborate evening of negotiations, the exchanged meals, the new garments ordered and altered. The households had put real labor into the promise. Everyone who had cut cloth or gathered branches had acquired a reason to want the promise kept.

Fara returned to the gate with an empty tray and told Noll not to lean on the arch. It would hold the branches, not him. She had already placed the dishes so the beans could be served before they cooled. If the ceremony was delayed much longer, she would begin feeding people. The paid meal did not require the bride to stand hungry for the sake of the cloth.

The old woman under the pear tree pointed her stick at the half-filled table.

“Where is the girl?”

Serra answered from the other side of the yard. “Dressing.”

The old woman made a small noise of disbelief.

“Then she dresses slowly.”

“Her hem needed doing.”

“She has had a hem for twenty years.”

Several people laughed. Serra did not. She folded a spare length of cloth and placed it on the arch in case the branches needed binding again. She had begun to inspect the gate after every new arrival. The smile she wore when she asked after someone else's health disappeared the moment that person passed her.

A little after the food was set out, a woman entered by the side lane without a green strip or a yellow flower. She was tall, with a pair of strong boots and a dark work dress that had been brushed clean but not adorned. She carried a small parcel under one arm, wrapped in a faded cloth. Her hair was bound in a plain knot at the back. She stopped before the arch.

Serra saw her first.

“Lysa.”

The young woman looked at the branches. “You put them up.”

“Of course. Your mother gave me the cuttings.”

“They're good branches.”

“Then where is the rest of your dress?”

“At home.”

“Someone should fetch it.”

“No one needs to fetch it.”

The courtyard grew quiet by a degree, not all at once. People nearest the gate heard; people near the food went on talking until they noticed that their own voices had become the loudest thing. Corin emerged from the side of the table and stopped halfway across the yard.

Lysa looked at him rather than at her aunt.

“Can we speak before you take your place?” she asked.

“Here?”

“If you want.”

Serra stepped between them. “The witnesses are waiting. You can speak afterward.”

“I asked him.”

“You have been speaking for weeks.”

“Then another moment won't break the roof.”

It was the first time Jake had heard the bride's voice. It had none of the tremor he might have expected from the talk around her. He did not presume she felt calm; he could see only that she was standing with both feet planted and that she would not let Serra answer for Corin.

Corin glanced toward the assembled households.

“Would it be better if we spoke somewhere private?” he asked.

Lysa shook her head. “I want you to hear me plainly. I don't want anybody to say later I told you something else.”

The old woman under the pear tree leaned forward. Nobody tried to move her out of hearing.

Serra's hand went to the strip of cloth on the arch. She tightened it though it was already secure.

“Don't make a spectacle of a little nervousness,” she said.

Lysa gave a small nod, as if the older woman's statement had answered one question she had been turning over for a long time.

“That's what I was told it was,” she replied. “And I believed it was small enough that I could make it go away.”

She set her parcel on the end of the table. A narrow ring of pale wood lay inside the cloth, the sort used to fasten a cord around a bundle. It had been cut but not polished.

“I brought this back,” she told Corin. “You gave it to me as a token of what we were going to do. It wasn't mine to keep.”

Corin did not reach for the ring. Jake watched the groom's hands curl and relax at his sides.

“Why are you giving it back?” he asked.

“Because I haven't said I will marry you.”

There was no scream, no overturned bench, no dramatic noise to cover the words. Their simplicity gave them a force that made every little sound in the courtyard distinct: the rasp of a branch on stone, a spoon tapping a bowl, a bird testing its voice in the pear tree.

Serra stared at Lysa as though the young woman had spoken in a language she knew but refused to recognize.

“We settled this,” she said.

“Not with me.”

Corin looked from one woman to the other. “You told me you needed time.”

“I still do.”

“You said after the roof was done—”

“I said I would think about it after the roof was done.”

Daro moved toward them. He raised one hand, palm outward, and told the guests that a private family matter would be settled before the meal. Jake wondered whether the words would have been just as confident if there had been no guests to hear them.

Lysa took a step away from the arch. She did not leave. Corin stood across from her, the pale wooden ring between them, while the food began to cool.
### III. The gate that stayed open

Serra was the first to try to turn the words back into a ceremony.

“A young woman may become afraid of the threshold,” she told the courtyard. “That is why the elder women walk with her. We don't name the fear a decision before we've carried her through it.”

“I'm not afraid of the threshold,” Lysa said.

“Then you have no reason to refuse it.”

“I didn't say that either.”

The aunt made a small sign with two fingers against her breast. Jake had seen the gesture at market disagreements and once beside a sick animal, but he could not have said what the sign meant to the person making it. Here it looked like an appeal to an unseen witness more patient than the people standing in the yard.

Corin reached for the small wooden ring and stopped before his hand touched it.

“Did somebody ask you to bring this back?” he said.

“No.”

“Did you decide it this morning?”

“No. I decided before you came to my house for the last supper. I meant to tell you then.”

“Why didn't you?”

“Your father was there. Mine had come over. The roof men were waiting for their payment. People spoke about the new shed as if it had always belonged to both houses.”

“You could have asked us to leave.”

“I could have. I didn't.”

She did not try to make the delay noble. Jake watched her leave the sentence where it stood, and for a moment the rest of the courtyard had nothing to hold it up.

Corin looked almost ill. He had come dressed for a vow, prepared for a day in which all uncertainty would be put behind him by words that had been practiced. Jake knew the feeling of approaching a room with an answer memorized and finding a different question on the table. The groom's distress did not make Lysa's answer less hers.

“I thought we wanted the same thing,” Corin said.

“I wanted the shed repaired. I wanted to keep working beside you. I thought I might want the rest.”

“You accepted the ring.”

“I took it to think about.”

“I carved it for you.”

“I know. I kept it. I polished half of it while I was thinking.”

She opened the cloth and showed him the rough edge opposite the smooth one. He leaned in without touching it. Jake could see the uneven surface where the knife had left narrow facets. The object had acquired two different histories in the hands of the two people who had passed it between them.

Daro stepped between the groom and the table.

“We've heard enough of this in front of outsiders,” he said. “Noll, take the young ones into the lane. Fara, cover the food. We will return when there's an agreement.”

“Agreement about what?” asked the old woman under the pear tree.

Daro did not answer her. He looked toward the gate.

“Close it. Let the families speak without half the settlement walking through.”

Jake was nearest the latch. He put a hand on the wood. It was an ordinary gate, fitted with a sliding bar and a loose peg where a latch had once been. The branches of the arch were tied above it and threw a trembling shadow on the wall. He could close it to keep new visitors from crowding the courtyard. He could do it without intending to hold anybody inside. He could also see that Lysa was standing between the table and the only open way to the lane.

“Jake,” Daro said, impatient now.

Jake eased the gate inward until it no longer caught the passage, but he left the bar lifted.

“It's open,” he said. “I can keep newcomers from pushing past the food, if you wish.”

“I asked you to close it.”

Corin spoke before Jake could find another answer.

“Leave it.”

Daro turned. “This isn't your father's way of settling matters.”

“My father isn't the one making vows.”

The groom had said it quietly. The courtyard heard because nearly everyone had stopped moving. Lysa looked at him without gratitude or triumph. He had not rescued her from a doorway. He had merely refused to make the doorway serve as a wall.

Daro took his hand from the gatepost. “You will regret humiliating your own people.”

Corin did not answer. He turned to Lysa instead.

“If you knew before the supper, why did you let us plan all this?”

“Because I believed I could persuade myself. Because people had carried wood, paid for paint, sewn cloth, argued over bowls. Because I liked you well enough that I hated saying no.”

The aunt gave an involuntary sound of disbelief.

“Liked him well enough,” Serra repeated. “As though we invited the houses together for a passing fondness.”

Lysa looked toward her aunt. “You invited the houses together because the shed was dividing them. We can keep a roof without making ourselves another piece of timber.”

“You don't know what it cost to settle that quarrel.”

“I carried the old rafters. I know some of it.”

That answer stopped Serra longer than the others. Her own hands had stitched the tablecloth and bound the sprigs above the gate; she might have forgotten that the bride had labored at the roof from which everyone wished to draw a new family. Jake could not know what she remembered. He saw only the aunt pull the loose thread from her cuff and twist it so hard it broke.

Noll moved toward the young men at the gate, as Daro had instructed him, then stopped. He had introduced Jake to the work, arranged the table, carried the arch and made himself useful to a dozen people who were not his relatives. There was no instruction here that would make the day simple again.

Fara came out of the serving corner with a ladle in her hand.

“Do you intend to eat?” she asked.

Daro stared at her. “This is hardly the moment.”

“The beans are cooked. The bread is cut. The households paid for them yesterday. If you want them cold, say so, and I'll stop fussing with the pot.”

Serra said, “There may still be a wedding.”

Fara looked toward Lysa, then Corin, then back to the aunt.

“Then ask the people who would be married. I have no authority over their mouths.”

A low murmur crossed the assembled guests. Some of it was outrage; some was relieved laughter; much was the uncomfortable sound of people discovering that there was no proper place for their hands. The two groups who had arrived in green and yellow stood apart for the first time since entering the yard.

The old woman beneath the pear tree struck the ground with her stick.

“I came for a feast. I was told there would be a wedding. Those are two separate promises. Which one can you keep?”

Corin looked at the food. The red color in his face had gone uneven, leaving him pale around the mouth.

“I can't say vows today,” he said.

He spoke to everyone, but Jake saw him glance at Lysa before he finished.

“Not with someone who has told me she will not. I would rather be ashamed of an unfinished wedding than speak for both of us.”

Lysa placed the little wooden ring on the table and moved her hand away.

Serra closed her eyes. Daro looked past the gate into the lane, as if there might be a person approaching with an older authority sufficient to undo the afternoon. No one came.

Fara took the cover off the beans.

“Then eat,” she said.

Corin stood still another moment. He had not acquired consolation simply by making a decent decision. When the first guest came forward with a bowl, he stepped out of the way. Lysa also moved, but toward the serving corner, where there were dishes to carry and no ceremony left to perform.

The table remained exactly the length Noll and Jake had measured, though the day it had been built for had already ended.
### IV. A feast can outlive its occasion

Fara had expected to serve the food after two people spoke a few ceremonial sentences. Once that order failed, she discovered that the guests were unwilling to make a new one. They stood beside the table without taking bowls, as if the food had been placed there to be admired, and one child began to weep from hunger.

The old woman with the sticks solved the first problem by taking a bowl from the stack and presenting it to Fara.

“Fill it,” she said.

“Beans first or onions?”

“Whichever is hot.”

Fara gave her both. The old woman ate her first mouthful standing, then reclaimed her shaded stool. The example worked better than anyone's argument. People began to approach the table, carefully at first, then with the greedy relief of guests who had been afraid of being the first to admit they were still hungry.

Jake carried a basket of bread to the far end of the table. Noll came with a tray of bowls. They did not attempt to arrange the guests by green and yellow, though Serra had set two rows of cups in alternating colors. A young man with a green band asked where he was supposed to sit if there was no married pair at the head. The woman beside him said he could sit wherever his knees would fit. He sat by a person wearing yellow. They spent the meal arguing about the best place to dry onions.

Lysa had gone to the serving corner. She took bowls from Fara's hired hand and passed them down the narrow space behind the table. The hired hand asked whether she was being paid for it. Lysa said no.

“Then don't push me out of my place,” the woman replied. “I'm the one who was hired.”

Lysa stepped back. There was enough room for two people at that end of the table only if one stood still and let the other work.

“I thought I could help,” she said.

“You can carry the empty bowls from the other side.”

The instruction was plain and unresentful. Lysa went around the table and did it. Jake watched her cross from a position of ceremony into the ordinary business of a paid meal without anyone declaring the change symbolic. The hired hand had her own work to protect. Lysa had hands she could use without taking it away.

Serra did not eat. She gathered the spare cloth from the arch and folded it precisely, the same way Jake had seen Ina fold the unfinished blue coat before Pell left for the hauling job. The resemblance was only in the movement. He stopped himself from making the two women into the same story: Ina's son was missing and her garment awaited a future neither she nor anyone could know; Serra's niece had spoken in front of them, and the speech had made a future impossible by choice. Both women had work to do with cloth, but the cloth could not be evidence that their losses were alike.

Daro approached the groom. Jake heard enough to understand that the uncle wished Corin to say something to the guests to quiet the gossip.

“You have to make it clear there was no deceit on our side,” Daro said.

“I don't know what to tell them.”

“You tell them the household kept its word.”

“Whose word?”

Daro's expression hardened. “Your family's.”

Corin shook his head. “I heard Lysa say she needed time. I thought she would come around. I can't say she broke a vow she didn't make.”

“Then you make us all look like fools.”

“I may be one,” Corin replied. “I won't speak for the rest of you.”

He returned to the arch and untied the green and yellow strips from one side. The branches sagged. Jake moved toward him and held the far end so he could free the last knot without tearing the twigs. When the arch came down, Corin carried the branches to a shaded corner. He did not crush them. A pair of small children asked whether they might use the straightest ones for a game. He told them to ask the owners of the courtyard. The children went looking for someone who knew.

Serra saw the empty gate and came over with the cloth in her arms.

“You could have waited until people left.”

“I couldn't stand looking at it,” Corin said.

“It took your cousins an hour to bind.”

“I know.”

“Then you should have thought of them.”

“I have.”

The sentence was not an argument she could easily defeat. She turned toward Lysa, who was setting down a stack of cups.

“Do you understand what you've put on Corin?” the aunt asked.

“Yes.”

“Do you understand it may not come off in a day?”

“Yes.”

“Do you imagine your mother can go to market tomorrow and nobody will mention it?”

“No.”

Serra seemed to have prepared for a defense and found none. She lowered the folded cloth, though she did not put it down.

“Your mother worked half a season for this dress,” she said.

“I know.”

“She wanted to see you wear it.”

“I told her I would wear the dress. I didn't understand that she'd think it meant the vows were settled.”

“Then you didn't tell her enough.”

“No,” Lysa said. “I didn't.”

The aunt's anger had not been misplaced in every direction. The years of care, the sewing, the weight of a celebration worked toward a conclusion that had failed. Jake could not find in that failure a rule that made Lysa obliged to marry. He also could not find a word that would refund her mother the hours spent on a garment she might never see her daughter wear.

Serra looked into the yard. The green and yellow guests were eating together now. Their mingling seemed to anger her more than the earlier division, as if shared food were an insult to the ceremony she had tried to preserve.

“You could have left before we invited them,” she told Lysa.

“I could have.”

“What were you waiting for?”

“I thought if I stayed, I would become the person you all saw.”

The aunt turned away. She carried the cloth to the gate and stood under the place where the branches had been. Lysa did not follow immediately. She finished carrying the cups. It was not a grand gesture. It allowed the hired hand to serve the last guests before the food cooled.

Noll stood beside Jake with an empty tray.

“I told Corin the roof would hold if the wedding took place,” he said.

“Does it fall now?”

“No. The carpenters did good work.”

“Then the roof will outlast us.”

Noll gave him a weary look. “I was speaking about the families.”

“I know.”

Noll shook his head. He was not offended. He had wanted the table to fit, the people to come, the arch to stand, and the old quarrel to cease. He had managed the first three. The fourth was never his to promise.

A small boy returned a bowl to Jake and asked if this still counted as a wedding feast. Jake said he did not know. The boy regarded the empty arch for a moment, then said he would tell his mother it was the feast where no one got married. He seemed pleased to have found a sentence he could remember.

Corin heard him and gave a short, wounded laugh. Lysa, across the yard, looked toward the sound but did not come over. The space between them was not a dramatic distance. It was no more than the length of the table and the people still eating beside it. Neither crossed it.
### V. What remained when the guests were gone

By late afternoon, the fruit had been eaten and the courtyard had begun to recover the proportions of an ordinary yard.

A child gathered the fallen pear leaves beneath the table. Noll loosened the ropes at the trestles but did not attempt to move the boards until the last old guest had risen. A small knot of women remained by the gate, speaking softly with the persistence of people who were not yet ready to decide whether they had attended a calamity or an entertaining scandal.

Serra stayed until the end. She had put the folded tablecloth in a basket, leaving the bare boards damp in the shadows. Lysa stood beside her and offered to carry it. The aunt refused, then handed it over a moment later without explanation.

“Your mother is going to ask where you are,” Serra said.

“I'll go to her.”

“Are you asking me to come?”

“If you want.”

“I want to know what happened to the dress.”

“It is at home.”

“Then we have something to talk about.”

They left together, but not arm in arm. Serra walked first through the gate. Lysa followed with the basket. Neither had put on the colored strips offered at the start of the ceremony. Jake could not tell whether walking the same road meant that they had made peace, and he did not need to use that word before they did.

Corin remained near the pear wall. The wooden ring lay in his palm, the unpolished edge turned up. He had retrieved it after Lysa left it on the table, but he had not put it on a cord or in a pocket. One of his cousins asked whether he wanted to return the wood to Lysa's house. Corin said no. The cousin said that perhaps the ring would be useful for fastening a sack. Corin looked at him until the man apologized and went to help Noll with the boards.

Jake went to the near trestle. He and Noll had moved the table at the beginning of the day. They moved it again, carefully, to the shadow beneath the wall. The boards weighed no more now, though their purpose had changed twice in a few hours. Noll set a wedge under the longest one so rainwater would run away from its underside. Jake left the timber where its owner instructed.

Fara counted her bowls. There were two fewer than she had carried into the yard and one more cracked than she expected. Her hired hand found one missing bowl beneath the pear tree. The other had gone home with a guest. They were ordinary losses from a crowded meal. The houses had paid Fara her agreed price. No one asked her to give back the money because no vows had been spoken; she had cooked, served, cleared and kept the hired help at work for the hours arranged. She did not pronounce on the families' sorrow or their honor.

“We should have measured the yard before we built the table,” Noll told her.

“You should have measured how many people would come through the gate with full bowls,” she replied.

“We did that after.”

“I noticed.”

She lifted her last basket and signaled to the hired woman. They left without another remark on the failed ceremony. Jake watched Fara go with an unexpected gratitude. She had refused to make her food stand for the decision of two strangers. It remained food, and people had eaten it.

Corin approached as the men were putting away the cord.

“Did you see her leave?” he asked Jake.

“Yes.”

“Was she crying?”

“Not where I could see.”

“Good.”

Jake could have said something comforting. The groom had endured a public refusal and had not used the crowd to answer it. That deserved more than the easy phrases people offered the defeated, but Jake could not decide what words would be his to give. He waited.

“I'm angry,” Corin said.

“You have reason to be.”

“She let me buy the branches and ask people to come.”

“Yes.”

“She didn't lie when I asked whether she was certain. She always said she needed time.” He looked at the ring. “I wanted those words to mean the answer was nearly yes.”

Jake had made promises to himself from uncertain signs before. The urge to turn another person's hesitation into evidence was familiar enough to frighten him. He did not tell Corin that he was a better man for recognizing it. Recognition had not spared him the hurt, and the hurt had not yet made him wise.

“Will you speak to her?” Jake asked.

“I don't know.”

It was the only truthful answer Jake could hear in the evening. Corin put the ring away at last. He said he was going to his father's house and would send someone for the tablecloth that belonged to the other household, forgetting that Serra had already taken it. Noll corrected him. Corin thanked him without embarrassment.

As the courtyard emptied, two young men passed the gate arguing about what had happened. One said the bride had run away. The other said she had been carried off by a cousin who opposed the union. Jake followed them into the lane.

“She was here,” he said. “She spoke to Corin in front of everyone. She walked out with her aunt at the end.”

The first young man shrugged.

“Maybe that is how you'll tell it.”

“It's what I saw.”

The second considered him. “Well, she left him all the same.”

“She did,” Jake answered.

That was as much as he could say without speaking for her. The men moved on, already returning to their own version of the afternoon. Jake did not chase them. He had said what he knew. Tomorrow a story might arrive at the stoneworks with the wrong ending, and he might have to make the same correction again. He was not certain that would help.

He walked down the lane past the dye yard. Ina's cloth was still hanging beneath the eave. Eren's painted marks showed on the side of the cart, where they belonged. A woman was measuring an arm's length of blue cloth against her shoulder while Ina watched the fit. The unfinished coat intended for Pell was nowhere Jake could see; he had no cause to ask after it or its wearer. No carrier had brought a confirmed report to him of the empty cart's retrieval or the missing men, freight and second animal. The mare's recovery was not his to declare. The kiln passage remained sealed. He had earned no additional stoneworks wage that day, and the letter to Esi had not been confirmed delivered.

In the direction of Fara's house he heard dishes being stacked. Farther away, in an unknown yard, a child was practicing three notes on a reed pipe. The fourth did not come while he listened.

He thought of the wedding table, its cloth sewn for two households and its meal eaten by people who had not been given the marriage they expected. Lysa had come to the gate before the vows could be said. Corin had left it open when he could have made a different show of his hurt. Neither act finished the quarrel over the shared shed or returned the hours that had gone into the dress. They were not an ending anyone had ordered.

Jake reached the corner where the road turned uphill toward his lodging. A little of the late light remained on the stone. He knew the way without a lantern. He did not know whether the bride and groom would speak again, or whether their families would find room beneath the roof they had repaired together. He had seen enough to know the wedding had not happened. Anything more would have to belong to those who were still living with it.

He took the uphill path. Behind him the lane filled with ordinary voices, none loud enough to command the others to stop.

---

# The Bees in the Wedding Arch

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XXXIV candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive canonical owner-principal identities. His identification with any historical 2016 league scoring slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. Every other person, all speech and conduct, the bee swarm, arch, horticulture, customs, routes, institutions and material circumstances in this chapter are proposed secondary-world invention rather than authenticated ESPN/Flaim events, real-world biography or approved historical Character Canon/Atlas. Entering state: Chapter XXXIII's fictional wedding between Lysa and Corin did not occur; Lysa departed with Serra, Corin retained the unfinished ring, the paid feast proceeded, the two households' shared-shed disagreement remains unsettled and the arch was left above Fara's courtyard gate. Jake has earned no wage since his earlier bounded outside stoneworks shifts; Vessa's kiln passage is closed, Jake's shelter debts unpaid and delivery of his letter toward Esi unconfirmed. Pell, the driver, the second horse and freight remain missing, while the mare's recovery and the abandoned cart's retrieval remain unproved. No new 2016 competition facts are introduced.*

### I. An ordinary morning beneath an extraordinary weight

The branches had changed color in the night.

Jake noticed it first from the upper end of the lane, where the wall made the entrance to Fara's courtyard appear as narrow as a doorway. Yesterday the arch above the gate had been a scatter of young green leaves tied with pale cord. In the morning light its underside looked dark, almost furred, and a low sound moved through it that was too steady to be wind.

A woman carrying a basket stopped ahead of him. She put a hand before her daughter's chest without speaking. The girl had been walking quickly, looking toward the place where the wedding feast had been served. Now she came to a halt so abruptly that one of her sandals scraped on the stone.

The woman turned.

"Don't go under that."

Jake followed her gaze. Bees had gathered on the central branch of the arch. There were so many that they concealed the cord binding the wood together. Others moved along the leaves, dropping a few inches and rising again. In the cool shadow they seemed hardly to move until the sunlight found them. Then the shape changed in slow currents, a dark mass with hundreds of glinting wings at its edges.

He had seen swarms pass above fields. He had not seen one settle where a whole gathering of people had stood the evening before. His first thought was that the arch must be broken beneath the weight. His second was that he had no idea how much a swarm weighed.

Noll came out of Fara's side door holding a long broom. He carried it wrong for sweeping, the handle close against his shoulder and the bristles raised as though he intended to point at something high on a wall.

"Don't," the woman with the basket called.

"I haven't done anything."

"You look ready."

Noll lowered the broom. "Fara wants the back shutters opened. There are bees inside by the kitchen cup."

"Then why have you got a broom?"

"Because I was on my way to open the back shutters when I saw the arch."

From the courtyard Fara shouted that she had already opened them. Noll looked at the broom, as if uncertain when it had become evidence against him, and leaned it carefully against the wall.

Jake stayed on the uphill side of the gate. Only a few bees came as far as the stone beneath his boots. He moved his foot away from one that was crossing a pale chip of mortar. Its motion was unhurried. The ordinary smallness of the insect made the clustered bodies above it stranger.

The daughter pushed against her mother's hand.

"Are they here for the wedding?"

"That is not a question for me," the woman answered.

"Because everyone was here yesterday."

"Everyone was at your grandfather's funeral and bees didn't come there."

"Maybe they didn't like him."

The mother turned the child away before she could enlarge the comparison. They took the other lane, where the stone steps passed behind the dye yard. The girl looked over her shoulder until they disappeared.

Fara came out carrying the basin she had used to rinse cups after the feast. Her sleeves were pushed above the elbow, and there was a pale seam of flour along one forearm. She stopped when she saw how many people were standing beyond her own gate.

"If you're not eating," she said, "you don't need to stand in the passage."

Noll told her there was a swarm.

"I know there is a swarm. I've been listening to it since dawn. Did you think I was telling the pans to be quiet?"

"Someone ought to fetch a keeper."

"I sent Tavin for Keret before the first pot was put on."

Jake knew the name only because he had heard a man at the stoneworks speak of wax bought from a keeper below the eastern fields. He could not say whether it was the same person. Fara did not offer him the pleasure of pretending he did.

She examined the arch from beneath the doorway but did not step under the clustering bees. "That was supposed to be taken down last night."

Noll looked at the branches. "It was late."

"The feast was late. The arch could have stayed until morning. I didn't expect it to acquire tenants."

There were still traces of the wedding in the courtyard. A strip of yellow ribbon had caught under a table leg. The pale cloth that had covered the serving boards was folded on a chair, waiting for its owner. A wooden ring had been left on the outer sill, then taken away; the clean circle in the dust marked where something round had rested. Jake could not tell whether the mark had been made by that ring, by a bowl or by an entirely different object. He disliked that he had begun to see yesterday in everything.

Corin had left with his unfinished token. Lysa had walked out with Serra. Neither had promised anything when the guests dispersed. Jake had seen the two young men in the lane invent a flight and an abduction before the courtyard had quite emptied. He imagined what they would do with a hundred thousand bees and an arch tied for a wedding that had not happened.

The first new interpretation arrived before Keret did.

Daro, Corin's uncle, came from the direction of the shared shed in a clean shirt and boots marked with clay. He stopped beside Fara and watched the dark body under the leaves.

"They chose the wedding arch," he said.

"They chose a branch," Fara replied.

"Out of every tree in the settlement."

"There are trees at either end of my wall, and the branch hangs over a gate that hasn't moved since my grandfather used it. I haven't asked the bees which part persuaded them."

Daro did not smile. He turned so the small audience could hear.

"This is not a thing to throw away."

Fara put her basin on the ground. "Nobody said throw them away. I said find somebody who knows how to move them. I want my door back."

The air warmed while they waited. Bees passed at the edge of the gathered people and returned to the arch. Jake could hear the low body of the swarm even when no single insect was near him.

He had gone down the lane intending to ask whether Fara needed water taken to her wash steps. Instead he was standing among neighbors whom yesterday had given something to dispute and morning had given a new object to dispute it over. He considered leaving. It was not his wedding, not his courtyard and not his swarm. Yet Fara had looked directly at him when she said she wanted the passage free.

"Would you like the people to wait farther off?" he asked.

"Yes. Without giving them an explanation of the heavens."

Jake asked the nearest three to leave a width of clear lane for the keeper. Two did. The third wanted to know whether the bees might be angry if the arch was moved.

"I don't know," Jake said.

"Then why are we moving?"

"We aren't. We're leaving a passage for someone who knows."

It was not the kind of answer that drew applause. The man took his place by the wall, still dissatisfied. Jake was glad. A man uncertain about bees ought to be more cautious than pleased.

### II. The keeper with the empty basket

Keret arrived without the solemnity that Daro seemed to think the occasion demanded.

He was a narrow man with a whitening beard that grew more heavily on one cheek than the other. A shallow wicker basket hung from a cord over his shoulder, and he carried a second basket turned upside down like a hat. A boy followed him with a wooden stool and a folded piece of pale cloth. Neither was dressed for ceremony. The boy had the look of someone who had been hurried away from a half-finished breakfast.

"Where?" Keret asked.

Noll pointed at the arch.

"I can see the arch," Keret said. "Where's the trouble?"

Fara crossed her arms. "The trouble is that the arch stands over my door."

Keret went close enough to judge the swarm and then stepped away. He watched a few bees move into the sunlight and land on the rough joint of a gatepost. He touched nothing.

"Who tied the green boughs?" he asked.

"Two households," Daro said.

"Which two hands?"

Corin came down the lane before Daro could answer. He was in the same work trousers Jake had seen him wearing while he placed the branches yesterday, though his careful wedding shirt was gone. He stood at the edge of the clear space and looked up. His face had not had much rest.

"I did," he told Keret. "Noll brought the cord. I tied the boughs to the posts."

"How secure?"

"Strong enough for a day's weather."

"That's not how weather counts."

"Strong enough that I had to pull the cord tight against the bark."

"Good. Better than somebody saying a blessing and trusting it to hold."

Daro glanced sharply at the keeper, but Keret was examining the shaded end of the arch.

"The people on the other side need to keep well back," Keret said. "The gathering has made them restless. I can take them into a basket if they settle where I can reach, and if the branches can be kept still. I can't promise they will agree to my arrangements."

"Are you going to hurt them?" asked the boy who had brought the stool.

"No more than I need to avoid hurting them or us."

"That's not an answer."

"It's as complete an answer as I have."

Jake was drawn to the keeper's way of speaking. Vessa at the stoneworks had met questions with the same unadorned limits when men asked her to reopen the unsafe passage. Her refusal had cost people their wages. Here, too, there were people who wanted certainty from a man whose work depended upon accepting what he did not control. Jake tried not to turn that resemblance into a lesson about all occupations; it was morning, the basket remained empty and the work had not begun.

Keret inspected the posts. The wood was sound enough, he said, but the arch was not a branch still growing on a tree. It rested on cord and a pair of borrowed stakes. The front stake shifted when Noll laid a fingertip against it.

"You won't take that out while they're on it," the keeper said.

"I wasn't going to."

"Then stop showing me how easily you could."

The boy set down the stool. Keret took it from him and moved it twice before deciding where its legs would stand level. He asked for no one to climb it yet.

Daro brought the argument back to his preferred ground. "The branches belonged to the ceremony. I have witnesses who expect to see what has happened."

Keret looked at him. "You have eyes. So have they. They can look from the far wall."

"I mean the elder women. The houses have a right to know."

"They can know the bees arrived. They don't need to stand beneath them to believe it."

"Perhaps they have brought an answer."

"Perhaps," Keret said. "If they speak in words, I shall ask what they mean. Until then I have a swarm and a doorway."

Corin was still looking up. Daro turned to him.

"Your father ought to see this before anyone interferes. It changes what happened yesterday."

"No," Corin said.

The word came quietly enough that Jake almost missed it.

Daro frowned. "No?"

"It doesn't change what she said."

A bee settled briefly on Corin's sleeve. He stood very still until it lifted off. The keeper had not instructed him to do so; Jake could not tell whether it was caution or merely the wish to avoid making a new disturbance. Corin lowered his arm when it had gone.

The gathering shifted to let Serra pass. She had the spare wedding cloth over one forearm and a small bag tucked into her elbow. Her expression sharpened when she saw Daro, but she addressed Fara.

"I brought the cloth you asked after."

Fara thanked her and told her to leave it inside by the back door, not beneath the arch. Serra looked up then, apparently for the first time, and made the small breastward gesture Jake had seen her make during the interrupted vows.

"Where is Lysa?" Daro asked her.

"Where she chose to be this morning."

"Does she know?"

"About the bees? I expect the whole lane knows. You've gathered half of it here."

"She should come."

Serra's shoulders rose beneath her shawl. "You wanted her to do what other people required yesterday, and that did not turn out as you planned. I won't fetch her to look at a branch."

"She was supposed to stand under it."

"That is why it is still standing."

Fara asked them to move away from the gate. Her request contained no judgment on which household had spoken most fairly; she simply had a pan of dough behind the shutters and needed the boy to carry water into the courtyard by the back entrance.

The boy with Keret's stool offered to carry it. Fara accepted and led him around the wall, leaving the keeper to his measurements.

When Lysa finally appeared, she did not come in answer to Daro.

She was carrying a coil of narrow rope and a pair of long gloves made of tough cloth. Jake had seen neither at the feast. She stopped well outside the cleared space, looked at the cluster, then at the people who had gathered around it.

"Serra said you needed a long line for the far side," she told Fara.

"I sent Noll to ask for one."

"He stopped at our door on his way. I brought it."

She gave the rope to Fara rather than to Corin or Daro. Her gaze passed over the half-empty courtyard and rested a moment on the arch. No one could say from her face whether she found the sight beautiful or hateful.

Daro spoke before Fara could thank her.

"You see what has come to this gate."

"I see bees."

"They have settled where the vows should have been."

Lysa studied the wood. "If you mean to ask me to stand under them, no."

"Don't be ridiculous."

"Then tell me what you mean."

Daro raised his chin toward the keeper. "It may not be too late to reconsider what the day signified."

"I said yesterday that I had not agreed to marry Corin. I haven't changed that today."

The keeper drew a slow breath and moved his empty basket farther into the shade. He had apparently heard enough of the conversation to know that continuing his work required fewer voices rather than more.

"Whose rope?" he asked.

"Mine," Lysa said.

"Can you spare it for an hour?"

"Yes. I don't need it back clean."

"Then set it across the narrow lane with the loose end tied around that stone post. Leave the knot low enough for a child to see. Don't tie it to the arch."

Lysa did exactly what he asked. She waited until Keret had checked the line's position, then went back to Serra. Jake watched Corin step out of her way without prompting. The movement was small, nearly invisible to anyone intent on finding a sign. It left each of them standing on a different side of a clear passage.

### III. What the branch could bear

The first attempt failed before a bee touched the basket.

Keret set the stool near the gate and tested it with both hands. He had asked Corin to keep his distance unless called, and Corin obeyed. Jake took a place by the far end of the rope, where people arriving from the lower lane might otherwise have walked straight into the clearing.

The keeper lifted the inverted basket above his head. A soft pattering came from the woven sides as his fingers pressed the rim. He meant to bring it close beneath the mass on the arch, wait for the moving bodies to settle, and then guide as much of the swarm as he could from the branch. Jake could see only the first movements. Keret was close enough to the gate that the wall obscured his hands.

A dry snap interrupted him.

It was not loud. A twig at the upper end of the arch had pulled partly free where the leafy bough crossed the rope, and a stream of bees rose in the sunlight. The keeper lowered his basket at once.

"Back," he said.

The people nearest the gate moved, not elegantly and not all in the same direction. The woman who had arrived with the basket earlier put herself between the little girl and the arch. Noll caught the overturned stool as its legs struck the stone. Jake stepped sideways to let three men come past him and found himself almost against the wall.

The sound of the bees grew sharper. Some flew above the clearing, others settled again on the remaining branches. No one had been stung that Jake could see. He did not confuse the lack of a cry with proof that everyone was safe.

"Keep the children behind the rope," Keret said. "No running, if you please. They aren't hunting anyone."

Tavin had arrived with another boy, both panting from the lane. He began to tell the younger one that a swarm could cover a whole man in a breath. The keeper, without turning, told him that stories of that sort could be exchanged when the baskets were packed. Tavin looked offended, then uncertain, then set about helping the little girl find a place where she could watch without being at the front.

Daro stood close to the gatepost. He had raised one hand toward the loosened arch as though to push the bough back into place. Corin put his own hand around his uncle's wrist.

"Don't touch it," Corin said.

"I'm trying to keep it from falling."

"Then let Keret tell us how."

Daro jerked his arm free, but he did not touch the arch.

Keret came down from the stool. He set the basket on the ground and crouched by the loose stake. The front of his shirt had darkened with sweat. He examined a split in the green wood and then the narrow line of bees that moved along it, patient where the men had not been.

"That was never a good tie," he said.

Corin began to answer, then stopped.

"It held overnight."

"Yes. And now it doesn't."

"I tied it."

"Then you've learned something about a fresh branch," the keeper said, in a tone too matter-of-fact to be either pardon or insult. "We need the weight off that end before I can take the rest."

Daro folded his arms. "You'll spoil the arch."

"The arch is not holding."

"It held for the ceremony."

"There was no ceremony," Serra said from the wall.

Daro's face tightened. Corin looked up toward the bees. Jake stood close enough to see the quick movement of his throat when he swallowed, but not close enough to have any right to declare what the sight meant to him.

A woman with two walking sticks came to the far end of the rope. She was the same old guest who had refused Noll's stool repeatedly at the feast and finally accepted the place beneath the pear tree. Her basket of dates was gone. Instead she wore a hat so broad that she had to tilt it to look under the arch.

"You have made a good crowd for a bad bridge," she said.

"There is no bridge here," Tavin told her.

"There was no wedding here yesterday, but I still got my supper."

She tapped the stone with one stick. When Jake offered to move a seat for her, she refused until she had decided for herself where to stand.

"What do the bees mean?" the little girl asked.

The old woman considered the cluster. "They mean somebody had a long night's flight."

Daro said they were gathered at a place of promise.

"If the bees could make promises," the old woman replied, "they would not need a keeper to ask them to move."

Her humor did not settle the quarrel, but it interrupted the feeling that everyone was waiting for a single authoritative interpretation. A man behind Jake began to argue that bees came to houses where a marriage would soon be made. Another said they came to houses where a marriage would be prevented. A third claimed they never came near green pear branches and must have been drawn by the food. Fara told them the food was gone and that nobody would be fed for standing idle in her lane.

Keret chose that moment to give his instructions.

"We will not save the decoration," he said. "The bees may be saved. The gate can be saved. If you want the green wood afterward, take what is left of it. But I cannot work with a branch hanging by one weakening tie."

Corin nodded. Daro did not.

"It was put there for the two houses," Daro said.

"I put it there," Corin replied. "I can take it down."

"Your father paid for the cuttings."

"He can have every branch that comes down."

"He might want them left up."

Corin glanced toward the lower lane, where his father was not among the assembled people.

"He can tell me that himself."

Jake could hear how much the statement cost Corin in the hush that followed it. He could not be certain it was defiance rather than exhaustion, and he would not have said so to anyone. But Corin had moved from receiving others' directions to giving one of his own.

Lysa stood beside Serra, the loose end of her rope coiled in one hand. She did not come to rescue the groom's choice from its consequences. When Daro appealed to her to confirm that the arch had been made for both households, she answered, "It was." When he asked whether it should be preserved, she said, "Not with the bees on it."

"You think you can wipe away a day because you didn't want it."

"No," Lysa said. "I think it happened. I was there."

The words struck Jake more than he expected. Yesterday had been an event, though not the event the families had ordered. The turned table, the failed vows, the consumed feast, the anger: none of them could be undone by pretending that the arch signified a different promise. He remembered his own failed attempt to correct two gossiping men in the lane and wondered why he had expected a true account to travel more swiftly than an exciting one.

Keret fetched a length of clean cloth from his boy and asked Noll to hold it ready but not wave it. He wanted to make a shaded place for the basket while a different approach was tried. The loose bough would be eased down only after the swarm had begun to gather elsewhere, if it chose to do so.

"Aren't you afraid?" Tavin asked.

"Of bees? Sometimes," Keret said.

"Then why do you keep them?"

"Some days the honey is worth the fear. Some days it isn't. The question is whether I can do the work properly while I'm afraid."

Jake found himself listening with the earnest attention of a man who had recently stood before a sealed kiln passage and been unable to answer what made it safe. He had no more claim to the keeper's courage than to Vessa's knowledge. The most useful thing he could do was keep the lane clear and listen when the man who knew the work said stop.

A small dark bee came down to the knot in Lysa's rope and rested there. For a moment the human argument ceased near her, and she waited for the insect to leave before she tightened the line.

### IV. The basket in the shade

They waited until the noon light had passed from the cluster.

The waiting lasted long enough for Jake to notice the work of the settlement continuing outside their little circle. A baker's boy carried loaves along the outer lane without stopping. Two women went by with washed cloth balanced on their shoulders. From the direction of Ina's dye yard came the knock of something wooden against a vat. No one there had abandoned the day merely because a wedding had failed or a swarm had settled. Even the crowd thinned when Fara announced that she meant to open for the midday meal and would not conduct her business through a ring of idle bodies.

Keret sat on the low wall and ate a piece of bread the boy had brought. He gave the boy the larger portion. Then he returned to the gate, bringing the inverted basket beneath the green branches once more.

Jake could not see all of what happened from his place by the rope. The keeper shifted the stool again. Noll held a piece of cloth between two hands, making a patch of shade against the wall. Corin stood ready at the far side, where he could support the stable upright without shaking the arch itself. When Keret called, he lifted one hand and took some of the loose strain away from the weakening tie.

This time the keeper had the basket properly placed before touching the hanging mass. A great part of the cluster gave way into it with a sound that Jake felt through his soles more than heard. There was a moment of sudden movement: bees darkening the lip of the basket, bees rising above Keret's head, bees flying to the green branch as though the thing they had left was the only certain place in the world.

Keret did not triumph. He lowered the basket to the stool and turned it slowly, making room for the moving bodies. He watched their paths. Then he set the basket on a level stone in the shadow beyond the gate, far enough from the passage that the people could retreat without crowding it.

"A good part of them are in," he said.

"All?" asked the little girl.

"No."

"How do you know?"

"Because I can see the ones that aren't."

She considered that for a while. "Will they follow?"

"Some may. We will give them time."

A narrow stream of bees moved from the arch toward the shaded basket. More wandered in the air and returned to the branch. Keret waited again, this time almost motionless. The crowd had expected an instant proof of his skill and now had to accept that success could arrive by degrees.

One bee found a way through the loose cuff of Jake's shirt. He felt the crawling on his wrist, turned his hand and held it still. A second later there was a sharp, small pain. He drew breath but did not slap at the place. The insect fell free when he shook the sleeve carefully. He stepped farther from the lane, rubbing his wrist with the other hand.

"You've been stung," Tavin said, delighted to discover a reportable event.

"Yes."

"Does it hurt?"

"Yes."

"How much?"

"Enough for one bee."

Tavin seemed disappointed that the answer did not scale up into a terrible account of the entire swarm.

Keret inspected the wrist briefly when he passed and told Jake to wash it and leave it alone. Jake complied at Fara's wash bowl, where the cold water relieved the first sharpness. The mark remained no more dramatic than a little raised spot. He did not turn it into a story of bravery. He had been standing too close to a bee.

When he returned, Keret was considering the few insects still moving along the underside of the arch. Corin was no longer holding the post. Daro had come forward again, but stopped short of the rope.

"Will you be finished now?" Daro asked.

"With the bulk of them, perhaps," Keret answered. "The rest may find the basket. I won't cut the branch while they are circling it."

"We have waited all morning."

"The bees have been at this longer than you."

Daro looked at the green arch. "My brother will say I let the whole thing be taken apart without asking."

"You can tell him why," Corin said.

"He'll want to know why you allowed it."

"I tied it. I gave leave to take it down."

"You gave leave as if the choice were yours alone."

"The gate belongs to Fara. The branches belonged to two households. Neither gives us leave to keep bees over her doorway."

Fara, hearing her name, called from the kitchen that she agreed with the last part and would be grateful if they settled it before her customers arrived hungry.

Daro stepped away. He did not bless the work or curse it. Jake could not say whether he had accepted Corin's answer. The space between them was plain enough.

Lysa came to the rope with Serra. She had been sent away once by a woman who thought the bride's presence might unsettle Corin. She had returned by the longer lane with a folded cloth of her own and now stood with its corners tucked beneath her arm. When Keret asked her to shift the rope so that the boy could carry away his spare basket, she did so. When he finished, she returned the line to the stone post and waited.

Corin approached the far end of the clearing. He did not cross the rope until Keret had told them they could stand farther up the lane. Lysa remained where she was.

"I thought you'd gone," Corin said.

"Yesterday?"

"This morning."

"I went home. I slept there."

"I meant farther than home."

She looked at the gate. "I have work here. There are people here I want to see. I wasn't leaving the settlement."

Corin glanced toward Daro, then back. "People said you would."

"People said many things."

"I said some of them."

That surprised Jake. Corin had not looked at him, and he did not approach to include him in the conversation. Jake moved a few paces toward the wash steps. He could still hear their voices when they raised them, but he did not turn the moment into his property by staying at their shoulder.

"You said I was certain," Lysa replied.

Corin answered quietly; Jake could not make out the words. A cart rattled over the uneven stones on the next lane, drowning a sentence. When its sound faded, Lysa was saying, "I should have told you sooner. Not everyone else. You."

"Yes."

"I knew you would be hurt."

"I was hurt anyway."

She held the folded cloth more tightly and then loosened her hands. Corin looked down at the worn toe of his boot. The basket beneath the gate hummed in the shade. Their silence extended beyond the small distance they had left between them.

"I don't want my uncle to speak for me," Corin said at last.

"Then don't let him."

"I can't make him stop speaking."

"No."

He gave a short laugh without much pleasure in it. He looked at Lysa and then at the upper lane beyond her.

"I need to go see my father. Not to tell him there's going to be a wedding."

"I can't help you with that."

"I know."

They did not clasp hands. Corin did not return the unfinished ring; it remained with him, out of sight, where Jake had last seen him put it away. Lysa did not offer a new answer to the old proposal. They stepped apart before any of the people around the gate began to admire their restraint as if it had been a ceremony of its own.

When enough of the remaining bees had moved toward the basket, Keret gave the word to loosen the last green bough. Corin kept the support upright while Noll undid the cord from the sound post. The branch came down in one piece and was laid beside the wall. Its leaves were bruised where the rope had pressed them. Daro picked up the smallest of the fallen twigs, turned it once in his fingers, and placed it with the others.

Above the gate there was only a pale scrape in the wood where the cord had tightened. Sunlight came through the space that had been filled with branches. For the first time since Jake arrived, he could see the entire lintel.

### V. The gate without an ornament

By the time the first customers came for their evening food, the bees had been taken to the shaded end of Keret's own yard.

The keeper made the journey with the covered basket in both hands, accompanied by his boy and Noll. He would return later to see whether the insects had stayed where he put them. He did not say that the swarm was now his, that it had become a proper colony, or that every bee had been recovered. When the little girl asked whether there would be honey tomorrow, he told her the first thing he hoped for tomorrow was that the bees would be alive and housed. She was at liberty to be disappointed by this answer.

Fara inspected the gateway. Noll had lifted the last fallen leaves out of the passage, but one length of wedding cord still hung from a peg. She took it down, wound it into a loose circle and placed it on the wall.

"Whose is this?" she asked.

"Mine," Corin said.

"Take it, then. I won't have a person catch an ankle on yesterday."

He collected the cord. Behind him Daro and another man had gathered the green branches into two bundles. The elder guest with the sticks was telling the other man that the best of them would still make a fire if he dried them first. Daro said they were not to be burned. The old woman told him that he could keep the twigs in a shrine if he wished, but he should not leave them against Fara's door where someone would fall over them. Daro lifted his bundle without answering.

Corin did not offer to carry it. He stood until his uncle had passed, then asked Fara if there was anything else left from the feast.

"The borrowed cloth went home with Serra. There is one bowl that isn't mine, and I have someone to return it to."

"What about the table?"

"Noll has already promised to help put it back."

Corin looked relieved at the simple inventory. Jake knew the expression only because he had just been relieved himself to hear an answer that did not require any more speech about vows.

The old woman followed Noll to the trestles, complaining that people had turned a morning's work into an exhibition. She gave him precise directions for carrying the end nearest her. He obeyed one instruction and ignored the next, which concerned the angle at which a grown man ought to bend his knee.

Serra returned to the courtyard for her bag. Lysa was beside her, still wearing the long gloves though the rope had been taken down. They stopped at Fara's door. She asked whether she might come by the next day to collect the small parcel she had left under a bench during the feast. Fara told her that if it was still there she would find it on the shelf with all the other things forgotten by people who ought to know their own pockets.

"Thank you," Lysa said.

"You may thank me when I've found it," Fara replied.

Serra was holding the folded tablecloth and watching the elder guest direct the trestles. Jake remembered how she had stood between Lysa and Corin before the attempted vows, trying to hurry the young woman beneath an arch and into a promise. Now she was holding household linen and had no ceremony to order. The difference did not make her gentler all at once.

"Your mother will ask why you brought the rope," she told Lysa.

"Because they needed it."

"She will say you should have stayed away."

"Then I can tell her I came and went."

"You don't have to explain every action."

"I didn't think I did."

Serra looked as though she might argue further. Instead she took the folded cloth into a firmer grip. Lysa removed one of her gloves and offered to carry the heavier bag. Serra surrendered it after a short hesitation, and the two of them went through the side lane at a pace that suited neither quite perfectly.

Corin watched them leave. He took two steps as though to follow, then halted by the gatepost. Daro called to him from the lower turn, telling him that his father expected him before supper. Corin answered that he had heard. He finished coiling the cord before he went.

Jake found himself with nothing required of him. Fara had her entrance, Noll had the trestles, Keret had the basket, Lysa and Serra had departed under their own power, and Corin was carrying a coil of cord into a conversation Jake would not hear. His wrist still ached faintly where the bee had stung him. It was a small wound that had cost no one else a remedy.

He went into the courtyard and bought a bowl from Fara. There was less to choose from than there had been during the paid wedding feast; she served him beans with greens and a piece of the bread made that morning. He paid from the money he had already earned at the stoneworks. He did not count the purchase as another wage, and Fara did not claim the meal settled anything beyond its price.

The little girl and her mother sat under the pear wall. The child had found a fallen leaf from the arch and was turning it between finger and thumb.

"Do you think Lysa will have another wedding?" she asked her mother.

"I don't know."

"Do you think the bees will come if she does?"

"Ask the bees when you see them."

The little girl considered the empty gate, then dropped the leaf into her own bowl. Her mother told her to take it out before she swallowed it. The child protested that leaves were food for some things. The woman said those things were welcome to eat their own leaves, but her daughter was to finish the beans.

Jake laughed before he could stop himself. The girl looked up, suspicious of being made the entertainment. He told her only that her mother had given a very fair answer. The girl examined him and returned to her supper. She had already lost interest in whatever lesson an older man might be tempted to draw from the bees.

Beyond the wall, the ordinary street grew busy. A pair of laborers went toward the stoneworks carrying rolled bedding. Their conversation concerned the price of a sharpening stone and an argument about which way to fit a handle. Jake could not tell whether either had work tomorrow. He had received no new order for an outside shift, and Vessa had not declared the unsafe kiln passage open. He was no more secure in his employment for having stood at the gate all day, and no poorer in debt than he had been at morning. The message he had paid Mev to carry toward Esi had not been confirmed delivered. None of those facts asked him to interpret the swarm.

At the empty end of the table Noll set down a folded cloth. He stood looking at the gate. The pale scrape where the cord had drawn tight remained on the upper post, and a few bees still passed near the wall, uncertain travelers that the keeper had warned would not all be gathered at once.

"Strange day," Noll said.

"Yes."

"We took a wedding apart without a wedding ever having happened."

"We took down branches."

Noll turned to look at him. "You've become careful with words."

"I have been wrong with them often enough."

Noll did not answer. He began to gather the smaller bowls. Jake helped him carry them to the wash steps, where Fara was setting out hot water. Neither of them moved the table without being asked.

When the work was done, Jake took the uphill lane. The arch was gone, but the gate stood where it always had, its bar loose in the socket and its painted surface worn by hands that had passed through for years before these two families had tried to join themselves. The evening light made the empty opening look larger than the narrow courtyard behind it.

He passed the dye yard. Ina's cloth hung under the eave, and Eren's painted marks were still visible on the cart. The unfinished blue coat for Pell was not in the window. That was not evidence of Pell's return or of his absence; it was simply a thing Jake could no longer see. No confirmed news had reached him about the missing freight party, the second horse or the cart in the high orchard hollow. The absence of news had not become good news merely because it had lasted another day.

At the corner he looked back. Corin was coming alone down the lower lane, no branches in his hands. Lysa was nowhere in sight. Fara was closing one shutter, while leaving the other open for the last customers. A few people walked through the gate beneath a lintel that carried no ornament and had nothing to promise them.

Jake turned uphill before any of them saw him looking. He could still hear the street, but not the bees.

---
