# The Street That Turned Blue

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XXXIX candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive canonical league-owner identities. The link between Jake and a 2016 historical scoring slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. All places, dialogue, craft, weather, social institutions and events in this chapter are proposed secondary-world fiction, not an ESPN/Flaim historical event, real-owner biography, verified geographical route, or approved Character/Atlas state. No interior viewpoint is assigned to a character outside the twelve owners.*

*Entering continuity: Mael has returned alive with an injured hand and admitted cutting a mare's trace, but the second horse, freight, cart and any carrier liability remain unresolved. Pell is at Ina's with an injured ankle and borrowed coat. Eight displaced travelers and one cart have departed with destination and safety unconfirmed; six, including Hessa and an infant, have stayed temporarily with their own cart at Fara's table house. The distant ash source remains unknown. Fara's inherited awning is permanently shortened, its flowered panel gone with the departed cart. The kiln passage is closed. Eren has completed and been paid for Ina's painted cart boards. Jake's earlier shelter debts, Esi's unanswered letter, Hessa's sister and the escaped bird remain open.*

### I. A color with nowhere to go

The blue was already in the street when Jake came out of Fara's courtyard.

At first he took it for a reflection. Morning lay in puddles among the paving stones, and a piece of sky had been caught in the shallow water where carts wore their ruts. But the sky above the roofs was the color of old pewter. The puddle shone with a blue so deep that the sunlight seemed to fall into it rather than strike it.

A child squatted beside the gutter and put one finger toward the water.

"Don't," said a woman from a doorway.

The finger stopped an inch above the surface. The child turned his hand over and inspected it, apparently disappointed by its continued cleanliness.

Jake looked along the line of the gutter. A narrow ribbon of color came from the turn beyond Ina's dye yard, passed beneath a bridge of two loose stones and vanished into the opening below the next house. A loaf crust drifted in it, half submerged. Wherever the water touched dry dust it left a darker edge.

The woman carried a broom with the bristles worn sideways. She did not come out of her doorway.

"Did she open a vat?" she asked.

"I haven't been up there."

"You ought to know where it goes before you put your feet in it."

"I wasn't planning to."

"Nobody plans to until it runs across the doorway."

She returned to her house. The child followed her, leaving the blue ribbon to slide between the stones.

Jake had been on his way to the stoneworks to ask whether a task remained after the early call. He could have gone around the upper lane and kept the color to one side. Instead he followed it. He did not tell himself that doing so made him responsible for the street. He was curious, and curiosity had already taken him farther from paid work than he intended.

Fara's table house stood behind him. Mael had slept there with his bandaged hand close to his chest, waking twice when carts passed outside. The six travelers were still at breakfast. Hessa had argued for a dry place to set the child's bedding, and Fara had pointed to the small strip of shade that remained beneath the cut awning. Neither had asked Jake to take charge. A pot of water stood covered in the kitchen, and the last he had seen of Fara she was cutting yesterday's bread into slices that would toast without much fire.

The first blue water did not appear to threaten anyone. It was beautiful enough to attract a child. That fact seemed worse when the stream thickened at the next turning.

Ina's yard was not far above the lane, though the passage toward it bent behind a row of houses that hid the work from the street. Jake heard the ordinary sounds before he saw the gate: the knock of wood against wood, a pulley complaining when a line was drawn taut, someone beating cloth against a board. The sounds had made the place familiar to him. He had watched Ina make her living there without ever learning the names of all the plants whose stains filled her hands.

Now a basin stood in the gate with a pale blue ring inside it. Beside the basin lay a strip of wool that might once have been white. Eren knelt near a low table, trying to coax a stiff brush through a narrow groove in a piece of painted timber. Her finished cart boards were not on the table. They had been fitted and accepted; the board under her hand was a small independent study, not a debt she was obliged to complete.

"Your street is escaping," Jake said.

She did not look up. "It isn't mine."

"Someone's color is."

Eren raised the brush and listened. He had not noticed the second sound beneath the hammering: a fast, irregular ticking, as if pebbles were being poured onto boards.

She stood in one motion. The brush slipped from her fingers and made a blue mark across the cuff of her sleeve.

"Where?" she asked.

Jake pointed through the gate.

Eren walked past him without stopping for her brush. From the lane they could see the stream making a little curl around the loaf crust. She crouched, held her palm near it without touching, and said a word Jake did not know.

"Is that bad?"

"It's ours." She rose, already turning back. "That part is bad."

Inside, Ina called for someone to bring the wide trough. Her voice was steady enough that Jake almost believed they had time.

Then the ticking became a continuous rush.

### II. The loose stave

Ina's main dyeing trough was long enough to take a length of cloth without folding it twice. It stood on stout blocks against the inner wall, close to the smaller vessels and the suspended rails where wet work could drip. One corner of the trough had moved. Water forced itself through a narrow opening at the join between a stave and the end frame, striking the lower paving in a hard stream.

Ina had placed two buckets beneath it. Both were full.

"Not the rail," she said when Jake reached toward a line. "The other end. Lift the empty tub away."

He obeyed. The tub weighed little until he tried to move it across wet stone; then its base caught at every uneven join. Eren seized the far handle and helped him turn it. A sheet of cloth lay inside, the folds dyed dark and pale in alternating waves.

"Where do you want this?" Jake asked.

"Anywhere the water hasn't reached."

Ina pressed her whole weight against the loose end frame. The wood had swollen unevenly and its iron fastening had pulled away from an old hole. The trough had been repaired before. The place where the new water found it was scarred with work a better morning might have kept hidden.

"We can drive it back," said an apprentice carrying a mallet.

"We can if we empty the trough first," Ina answered. "Not while it is pushing against us."

He looked at the mallet, then at the water. His hesitation cost nothing but a moment. Jake wished he had been as willing to lay down a tool when he first began work at the wheel.

There were three vessels on the yard floor and a fourth near the gate. The apprentice set his mallet aside, and the three of them began carrying liquid into whatever could safely hold it. Some of the bath went into a covered vat. More spilled because every vessel had to be lifted from beneath the jet and tipped or carried past the crowded table. The floor grew slick. Wet blue footprints appeared around the yard like evidence of a dance nobody had intended to begin.

"Don't put your hand in that," Ina called when the apprentice reached toward a falling strip of cloth. "Take the hook."

The cloth came free on an iron hook and slapped the paving. The sudden weight of water in its folds knocked the hook sideways. Jake caught the handle before it struck Eren. They laughed at the same instant, the quick foolish laugh of people surprised to find themselves unhurt. Then they looked at the stream running out through the gate, and neither laughed again.

"What's in it?" Jake asked.

"Enough to stain anything it meets," Ina said. "I will not tell you what it is safe to drink."

"I wasn't going to drink it."

"Neither was the street."

Eren had found the loose fastening. She knelt by the swollen frame and studied the old hole, running a finger along the wood grain away from the jet.

"The socket split," she said. "It won't hold another peg here."

"Then we drain it before we mend it." Ina looked toward the entrance. "Who has the empty barrels?"

"At the lower shed."

"Bring them if they are dry. If they are not, don't waste the walk."

The apprentice ran. Ina took the hook from Jake and used it to pull the last length of cloth clear of the moving water. Eren rolled it loosely on a board. The cloth's blue began to drip from the edge in thick, deliberate beads. Jake realized that the liquid leaving the yard was not merely an accident in a vessel. It was work that could no longer be done as ordered, color that would never enter the cloth Ina had meant to sell.

He tried to steady the broken frame. Ina stopped him.

"Leave it. There is nothing there strong enough to steady."

A small splinter gave way. The gap widened by less than a finger, and the stream doubled.

Eren stepped clear. Jake stumbled backward over the empty tub and sat down hard. He heard a terrible wooden knock from the trough and raised his hands to protect his face. The end frame held. The rush did not slow.

"Out of the way," Ina said, not loudly. She was looking at the lower gate, where the water had begun to escape in a sheet.

The apprentice returned without barrels. He had found them full of salted hides and no room to empty them. Jake saw the apology on his face before he spoke.

Ina took the mallet, went to the opposite end of the trough and knocked loose a smaller stoppered opening that drained into an old receiving vessel. It was not a repair. It was a deliberate sacrifice of the remaining bath to keep the broken end from failing all at once. Blue fell into the vessel, foamed over its rim and ran across the paving in two directions.

The trough stopped straining. The street kept receiving the color.

"Go after it," Ina said to Jake. "Not to save the dye. Tell people not to use the water where it comes through."

Eren seized the hook. "I'll bring the spill cloths."

"You'll bring only the dry ones," Ina said. "And don't chase the stream into a covered drain."

Eren nodded once. She did not ask whether the old bath could be made again. Jake followed her out the gate into the blue morning.

### III. At the mouth of the lane

By the time they reached the lower turning, the color had made the little street look freshly painted.

It did not move with the force of a flood. It was worse in a quieter way: a steady stream that found each depression and refused to stay within the path Jake would have chosen. Some of it disappeared beneath the house with the worn broom. Another part crossed the paving and ran around the foot of a wall toward the table-house lane.

A woman had placed three broken pots across the gutter to arrest it. The water slipped through the spaces between them. She stood back, furious with the pots.

"What have you brought us?" she demanded of Eren.

"A broken trough," Eren answered. "I'm fetching cloth to stop what I can."

"Whose trough?"

"Ina's."

"Then why are you the one telling us?"

"Because I was standing closest to the gate."

The woman was preparing another question when Eren laid her bundle of dry waste cloth along the gutter. The blue reached it and began climbing the fibers. Eren weighted the cloth with stones. It made a wavering barrier no taller than a hand, enough to slow the shallower water and push some of it toward the open ground by the wall.

"That won't last," Jake said.

"No," Eren answered. "Find something that will."

He went around the corner toward Fara's. He heard the child's voice before he reached her courtyard, a high delighted cry from beyond the bench. Hessa stood in the entrance with the infant against her shoulder. Beside her, the boat-cover maker from the remaining company held a length of coarse sailcloth stretched between two hands.

They had seen the blue water at the edge of the courtyard. Fara had already brought the serving bowls indoors.

"Not through the kitchen," Fara said.

"It isn't there yet," Jake answered.

"Then we have a chance of keeping it out."

She had set an empty bucket beneath the drip from her shortened awning, though nothing was falling from the sky. It stood there because she had no better place for it and because, since the fire, she had disliked leaving useful vessels out of reach. Jake noticed a faint dusting of ash still caught at the new stitch along the canvas. The painted flower that once hung beyond the outer post remained absent.

"What's blue?" Hessa asked.

"Water from Ina's broken trough."

"What else?"

"She said not to use any water it reaches."

Hessa looked at the infant, then handed the child to one of the two women who had stayed with her. She pointed to the covered kitchen pot.

"Keep that inside. Do not bring it to the door."

The woman took the child and went. Hessa turned to the maker.

"Can your cloth stop it?"

"It'll drink the first part," the maker said, showing the coarse weave. "Then it will pass the rest through. We need a slope that sends it somewhere else."

"Where?"

The maker walked out to the lane and inspected the paving. She squatted by the blue stream, sighting along it as one might sight a seam to decide whether a cut cloth could lie flat. The water ran toward the eating room's lowest step. Beyond the step the lane bent away into a rough patch of open ground that held weeds and stones.

"That way," she said, pointing. "But it won't follow a wish."

Fara brought out two lengths of timber from the stack she used to shore up tables. They were old and splintered, not fine beams. The maker put one across the gutter and angled the other toward the open ground. Jake fetched stones to hold their ends. Hessa laid the coarse cloth against the timber to soften the gaps.

For a moment it worked. The blue water turned, hesitated at the join and ran away from Fara's step in a thin line.

The child with the earlier curious finger appeared at the lane's far end. He had escaped his mother's doorway and was watching from the dry paving.

"It looks like a ribbon," he said.

"It is not one," Fara answered. "Go home."

He stayed just long enough to decide whether he could reasonably be offended by the reply, then went.

A boy brought a brush of cut reeds from the lower yard. He offered it to Hessa without saying anything. She thanked him and used it to sweep debris from the barrier. The work might have been comic if the sweep had not turned her sleeve blue to the elbow. Jake almost laughed. Hessa looked at the sleeve herself.

"I had planned to wash this today," she said.

"You can still wash it," Fara answered.

"In what?"

Neither woman smiled. They were looking at the covered pot inside the house, and Jake understood that every vessel they had kept clean was now more valuable for being separate from the street.

Then Eren came around the turn, carrying a wooden plank half again as long as herself.

"That needs to go above the corner," she said. "The water is finding another way in."

She set the plank down. It was one of the boards she had used to lay out painted designs, already scarred with old trials, not Ina's finished cart commission. Jake reached for it. Eren stopped him long enough to show the end that had been split by a nail.

"That side faces the stones. If it catches your ankle it will open it."

Jake took the safe end. Together they carried the board toward the turning.

They had not yet set it when the first blue water appeared at Fara's lower kitchen step.

### IV. What the current wanted

The water had found a route behind the wall.

It came not from the gutter they had barred but through a narrow seam where two houses met, a passage so small Jake had never thought of it as a passage at all. The ground behind it had been scraped lower by years of sweeping and rain. Blue slipped along the seam, trickled across the shaded stone and reached the edge of the basin where Fara usually rinsed her cups.

Fara lifted the basin away before the colored water reached it. The underside left a clean pale circle on the paving.

"Take that inside," she said.

Jake carried it across the room. He could hear the people outside moving the barrier, the slap of wet cloth and timber against stone. For a few breaths he was alone beside the long table. Someone had left a child's bread crumb at the edge of a plate. The kitchen smelled of toasted crust and the sharp green of herbs. No blue water had entered the cooking pot. He did not need to invent a greater catastrophe to feel his chest tighten.

He went back into the courtyard.

The boat-cover maker had rolled the coarse cloth and was pressing it into the seam. It held briefly. Then the water gathered above her hand and seeped along the wall, touching another crack. She withdrew and tested the stone with the back of her knife.

"Not solid," she said. "It will open wider if we hammer here."

"Then don't hammer," Fara said.

Hessa had brought a sack of dry grit from her cart. She opened it on the paving. It was valuable ballast and packing, not something a traveler could replace with a word of thanks.

"Spread it on the far side," the maker said. "Not in the mouth. Make the stream go around it."

Jake hesitated. He had been looking for a single place to stop the flow. The maker had spent a life making cloth repel rain, and she was trying to give the water a path. He moved the sack where she pointed.

The grit darkened and held. He pulled the longer plank into place. Eren set stones at its end and drew a rough line with her finger to show the direction she wanted the current to take.

The water turned again. It ran past the outer bench instead of beneath the kitchen step, blue against the cracked paving, and entered the rough open ground. A low pool began to form there. Nobody called it harmless. They had merely moved a problem from the threshold to a place where fewer hands would touch it.

Ina appeared at the bend in the lane, accompanied by the apprentice. The apprentice carried an empty bucket. Ina's arms were stained to the elbow, her apron dark with water.

"The trough is emptying," she said. "I have closed the first gutter, but the yard still holds a bath on the floor."

She saw the line of timber, the stained cloth, the makeshift grit bank.

"That won't hold the next rain."

"No rain yet," Fara said.

"Then it holds until we find another way. I'm not going to call the street clean because the dye looks pretty."

Eren wiped a hand across her cheek. She left a blue streak.

"Can we shore the frame?"

"Not before we find wood that hasn't split. You saw the socket."

"I could make a new drawing."

"You could. I need a cooper, not a drawing."

Eren absorbed this without retreating. She looked down at the plank she had contributed. Its painted trial marks had vanished beneath a blue flood of another kind. Jake expected her to defend her art. Instead she bent and tested the board with her weight, shifting one stone to keep the lower end from floating.

"I'm not done with this one," she said.

Ina looked at her for a moment. Then she came closer and laid the empty bucket at the bank.

"There is another drain behind my wall," she said. "I can block it with packing and stop more reaching this lane. But I won't be working wet cloth until we rebuild the trough and clear the ground. Not tomorrow. Not the day after, if the wood stays as it is."

"You have work waiting," Fara said.

"I have people waiting for the work. They will have to hear the truth of it."

The apprentice shifted the empty bucket in his hands. He had been carrying it back and forth as if its emptiness embarrassed him.

"What do I tell them?" he asked.

Ina looked at him. "Tell them the trough failed. Tell them I stopped it. Tell them I can't yet name a day when it will hold again."

His eyes went toward Eren. She was kneeling at the bank, pressing wet waste cloth between the plank and the stone. Her painting board, bought with her own labor, had become a soaked barrier without anyone having arranged a payment for its loss.

"Will you pay her for that?" he asked Ina.

Before Ina answered, Eren raised her head.

"I chose where to put it."

"I didn't ask who chose," the apprentice said.

"Neither did I," Ina answered. "We can speak of the board when the water has stopped moving."

For the first time Jake saw that the apprentice had not merely wanted his mistress to be fair. He had wanted to say something difficult in her hearing. Ina did not rebuke him for the question. She went back toward the yard to close her own second drain, leaving Eren with the stones and a choice she had already made.

The blue pool widened by a hand's breadth. They moved the last plank. The water drew a new curve across the ground.

### V. A morning spent elsewhere

The rest of the morning was not one heroic effort but a series of small failures that had to be noticed before they grew large.

The cloth at the seam clogged and overflowed; the maker took it out and replaced it. The first grit bank slumped; Hessa opened another sack, though she had been offered no new supply for her cart. Someone knocked loose a stone and sent a narrow tongue of blue water back toward the kitchen; Jake caught it with a shallow shovel and scratched a temporary channel to the wider pool.

Every correction left the ground uglier. The little open patch by the wall was no longer fit for sitting or setting down clean washing. Blue eddies circled the weeds, and the pale ends of roots appeared beneath the water. The earth's slope, invisible while it was dry, had declared itself in loops and channels.

Fara called for everyone to stop bringing wet cloth through her eating room. She moved the long table farther from the entrance and set clean water where the child and the six travelers could reach it without crossing the dyed paving. It was water she had stored before the spill. She would not refill it from the gutter, however many people asked whether the blue had faded.

A woman from the street arrived carrying an empty pail and an angry expression. The opening of her house faced the other gutter, the one Jake had followed at dawn.

"There's color in my laundry basin," she said. "I had the sheets out."

Ina, who had returned with the apprentice, listened without interrupting.

"I told them to draw from the covered store until we know where it ran," Ina said.

"What if it ran into the store?"

"Then don't draw from it. I cannot see through your wall."

The woman looked ready to answer sharply, then lowered her eyes to the blue line on Ina's apron. They spoke for several moments about which vessel had been covered and which had stood open. Jake was too far away to hear every word. He did not move nearer. A basin belonged to a household, and he had no reason to bring that household's account back to Fara's tables.

A little later the apprentice crossed the lane with the empty pail returned to its owner. The woman carried it inside. No proof of safe water came with it.

Mael came out from Fara's to sit in the corner of shade that remained. His injured hand was bound in fresh linen. He looked at the blue ground and said nothing about roads or broken carts.

"Can you help?" Jake asked, then regretted asking when he saw the bandage.

"I can watch where the water goes," Mael said. "That hand isn't good for a shovel."

He took the outer bench, which Fara had moved away from the pool, and sat facing the turning. His stillness became useful when he noticed a new trickle at the side of Eren's plank.

"It's coming under," he said.

Jake wedged a stone there. The trickle stopped.

A young girl from the remaining travelers approached carrying a closed jar. Hessa intercepted her at the door.

"Where are you taking that?"

"To wash the baby's cloth."

"Not there. Back inside."

"It's only blue."

"Then keep your hands clean enough to hold the child."

The girl carried the jar back without argument. A minute later she came out with an armful of dry bedding instead. She laid it on the sunny half of the courtyard, beyond the shortened awning. The sunlight was now useful in the place where the old shade had once reached. She put a stone on each corner to hold the bedding down. It was not an omen or a compensation. It was simply a dry surface in a crowded house, and she had seen it before Jake did.

The maker passed him a length of twisted cord.

"Would you bind this end for me?"

He knelt and held the plank while she lashed it to an iron loop in the wall. She checked his knot, pulled it loose and tied it again herself.

"Not your craft," she said, without malice.

"No."

"Then do the holding."

He did. He watched her fingers lay each turn of cord close against the last, keeping pressure where the plank might rise. Her work was exact even in a street that smelled of dye and wet grit. She neither praised his effort nor apologized for correcting it.

By midday the blue flow had dwindled to a shallow seep. At the upper gate Ina had sealed the second runoff opening and moved the broken trough's remaining vessels into a dry corner. There was no new stream entering the lane. The pool remained where it had been diverted, and the stain ran in thin lines between the stones all the way down to the turning.

Fara made a pot of barley and greens with the water she had kept covered. There was less than she would normally have served. She added bread and cut the portions a little smaller.

Eren washed her face with a damp cloth brought from inside. The blue streak persisted beside her eye.

"Do I look like the street?" she asked Jake.

"Worse. The street has two good sides."

She looked toward the pool. "It's not the street's fault."

"No."

She almost smiled. Then she sat on the outer step with her wet board in her lap and began prying the stones from its corners. The water had softened one painted trial until it came away on her thumb. She rubbed it gently, not to remove the color but to learn how much of the wood remained sound.

### VI. The work that was closed

Ina came down again after the meal and stood beside the bank.

She had changed her apron, but the nails of her hands still showed blue. The apprentice was with her. He carried a little wooden peg newly cut and not yet fitted to anything.

"The trough won't take it," Ina told him when he showed her.

"It fits the hole."

"The old hole. The split goes farther than the hole."

He turned the peg over. He had worked carefully on it. Jake could see that much in its clean sides. The apprentice put it in his pocket rather than throw it into the pool.

Ina walked to Fara's door.

"I can pay for dry water to be carried down," she said. "Until I know the yard isn't sending more color into the street."

Fara shook her head. "You can't buy the whole lane a new well by offering me one bucket."

"I wasn't offering you a well."

"Then tell me what you can offer."

Ina named two empty storage vessels, a covered place from which she could fetch clean water for the kitchen, and a day on which the apprentice could help move the stained packing away from the doorway. She did not say the stain would vanish. Fara listened, made her alter one part of the arrangement, and finally agreed that the vessels could be brought before supper.

Jake could hear the appetite for a greater reckoning in the people gathered at the corner. A man had begun to count the number of blue stones as though a count could restore the earlier street. Another said he had lost a day's washing. Neither was wrong to notice loss, but the vessels were still needed. Fara went indoors without making the street hear a judgment.

Hessa emerged with the infant awake and watchful in her arms. The other five travelers had begun to move bedding back from the sunny paving. Their cart remained at the wall, its donkey cared for but not yet readied to travel.

"We said one more night," Hessa told Fara.

"You did."

"We'll need another morning to set things right before we move the cart. The road's passable in one direction and soaked in another."

"I don't know the road beyond my door," Fara said.

"Nor do I. I'm asking for the morning here, not a promise of the next road."

Fara shifted the bowl she held beneath her arm. "The room will need cleaning. You can use it until then."

Hessa nodded. She had been asking for time, not a place to settle forever. She turned to the maker, who was testing the cord on the wooden plank. The two spoke briefly about folding the cart cover and putting the clean bedding where the dye could not reach it. Jake heard no announcement about Hessa's sister. No news had arrived.

Ina went back to her yard with the apprentice. Eren followed them partway, then stopped at the turning where the stream had first caught Jake's eye. She set her stained board against the wall to dry. She took out a piece of chalk and marked the height the blue water had reached upon the stone.

"What is that for?" Jake asked.

"So I don't lie to myself about where it was."

She moved the chalk to a second place along the wall and drew a shorter mark, where the water stood now. The distance between the two lines was only a few inches.

"Will you paint it?" he asked.

"Not today."

She left the chalk with the board and returned to Ina's yard. Jake watched her go. There was no speech to explain whether she would paint a picture of the day or keep the lines merely to show where the water had passed. The marks were enough for now.

He had missed the stoneworks call. His clothes smelled of the dye bath, and the skin between his fingers was dark from handling wet cloth and stone. He could go to the work yard tomorrow and ask again. Today nobody had assigned him four paid hours, and no coin had been promised for holding a plank. He found that this was neither a reason to resent the work nor a reason to tell people how generous he had been.

At Fara's door the child who had watched the ribbon of blue water stood beside his mother. She was holding his hand tightly. He looked at the two chalk marks and then at the blue line that curved into the waste ground.

"Will it stay?" he asked.

His mother looked down the street. "Some of it."

He appeared to consider that answer with the gravity of a child deciding whether a game had ended. Then he lifted his clean hand and pointed toward Eren's board.

"Will she make it into something?"

Jake followed the gesture. The plank was a ruin of painted experiments, propped to dry. He had helped soak it. He did not know what Eren would make of it after that.

"Ask her," he said.

The child took one step forward before his mother stopped him. The lane was still wet, and she would not let him cross it.

Fara called from the eating room for the clean bowls. Hessa answered. The boat-cover maker was loosening her knots from the timber so the wood could be reused when the water finally ceased. In Ina's yard a mallet sounded once, then stopped, as though somebody had tested a tool and decided the work could not yet begin.

Jake bent to lift the first clean bowl. He heard the blue water moving very softly beneath the stones. It had gone farther than any of them had seen. At the edge of the courtyard, the little open patch held its new pool, and the far bench stood in the sun where no unburned awning would return to shade it.

He carried the bowl indoors.

---

# The House Made from a Road

*2016 Commonwealth historical causal novel — Chapter XL candidate. NONCANON / INDEPENDENT EDITORIAL HOLD. Sole limited interior viewpoint: proposed fictional Jake / CHAR-JAKE-KALOPER / PRINCIPAL_CHARACTER, one of the twelve exclusive canonical owner identities. The association of Jake with any 2016 scoring slot remains UNAUTHENTICATED. This chapter invents a secondary-world household, dialogue, workshop, people, political pressure and material consequences: none is an authenticated ESPN/Flaim event, verified historical-owner motive, approved 2016 Character Canon state or Atlas geography. No new/revised interior POV is assigned to any person outside the Twelve.*

*Entering continuity: Ina's dye trough failed in Chapter XXXIX and her wet dye work is suspended. Blue runoff was diverted but the downstream route and local water safety remain unverified; separate covered cooking water is being used. Six displaced travelers, including Hessa, an infant, Orin and a boat-cover maker, remain at Fara's table house for one additional morning with their one cart and a tended donkey; eight others departed with a different cart, with arrival unknown. Fara's inherited awning remains permanently shortened. Mael and Pell have returned injured, but the second horse, freight, cart and carrier liability are unresolved. The distant fire and Hessa's sister's fate are unknown. Jake's older shelter debts, his unanswered Esi letter and the escaped bird remain open. The kiln passage is closed.*

### I. An offer measured in mornings

The day after the street turned blue, six travelers folded their bedding before anyone had asked them to leave.

Jake discovered the bundles beside Fara's outer bench. They were not arranged as a departure party would arrange them; each had been tied by a different hand, and some were still open, showing a wool sock or a child's cup or a little folded square of cloth. But there was something final about the clearing of the floor. The eating room looked suddenly larger. He could see the worn place beneath the table where somebody had once dragged a heavy chest.

Fara stood in the doorway with the cooking ladle in her hand.

"You told them to go?" he asked.

"No."

"Then why the bundles?"

"Ask them."

She returned to the kitchen. The ladle struck the rim of a pot, once, without the pleasant rhythm of someone preparing a meal. Jake had heard her say that the extra morning was theirs; he had also seen the rough count of bowls she made before supper. A promise that ended at noon did not become a promise for another night merely because the guests were still there at dusk.

Hessa came in from the yard carrying the infant and a length of canvas folded across one arm. She stepped around the bundles without looking at them.

"We've taken the room too long," she said.

"Fara offered the morning."

"We've had it."

"Your donkey's still here."

"The stable keeper's checking its feet. We will pay him for that."

Jake watched the child close and open a tiny hand against the canvas. The infant's eyes stayed on his face, making a kind of inquiry for which he had no answer. Beside the far wall the boat-cover maker was rolling her tools in a strip of leather. Orin counted the pins that had held the window cloth, touching each one with his thumb before putting it away. The other two travelers were outside with the cart. None had asked Jake to direct the packing.

"Is the road clear?" he said.

"We don't know."

"Then why move?"

"Because not knowing does not make this room ours."

It would have been easy to call that stubbornness. Jake had made the same argument for himself at the shelter, once when a bed had been offered and later when the bed had been given to someone more injured than he was. He had been proud of his refusal in the moment and hungry by morning. Hessa was not asking him to approve her pride. She was naming a boundary he was tempted to overlook because he did not want to watch another departure.

The road beyond the dye yard was damp beneath a dull sky. The blue stain had lost its brilliant surface. It had entered the pores of the stones and made them look bruised. At the bend where Eren had drawn two chalk marks, the lower line had smudged under the night's damp. No one had measured how far the wash went after leaving the street. Fara kept the drinking vessels covered. Ina had sent the agreed storage jars, empty and clean, but had not pretended that their arrival restored the water that was lost.

An apprentice came down from Ina's yard carrying a coil of rope. He passed Fara's gate, stopped when he saw the bundles, and turned back toward the workshop without speaking.

"He's afraid his work has ended," Jake said.

"Maybe it has," Hessa replied. "That is his trouble to tell us about, if he wishes."

Her words stayed with him. They seemed severe until he remembered how often he had explained other people's troubles to them, as though the explanation were a service. He had not been the one to stand beside a ruined trough and decide whether the shop could open. Nor had he been one of the six who must fit their lives into a cart before the sun climbed above the wall.

Ina arrived while Hessa was still fastening the canvas. She wore an old work shirt, the sleeves rubbed pale at the elbows, and had neither a bucket nor the stiff brush she usually carried. Her hands were empty.

"I have a dry room," she said.

It was such a simple statement that nobody answered it.

"Above the dye shelves," Ina continued. "Not over the broken trough. It has a roof, a door that shuts, and space where we used to set the cloth frames in wet weather. I haven't put anyone in there. I won't call it a lodging until you've seen it."

Hessa looked first at Fara, who had followed Ina to the threshold.

"You're offering them your workshop?" Fara asked.

"A room in it."

"For how long?"

"That is what we would have to decide."

Hessa set the sleeping child more securely against her shoulder. "Why?"

Ina glanced toward the stained street, then away. "Because I can't dye cloth there this morning. Because I may not be able to next month. I would rather know what the empty room is for than let it sit above tools I cannot use."

Nobody mistook that for a complete bargain. It was an opening, and an opening could still close.

### II. The room that had been work

They went up through Ina's yard by a stair attached to the dry side of the building. The familiar odor of wet wool and dye was fainter here, caught in old boards instead of rising from working vessels. Jake could hear footsteps overhead when he stood beneath the stair. A small quantity of finished cloth hung on pegs outside, high enough to stay clear of the blue-wet stones below.

Ina opened the upper door with her shoulder. Daylight entered through two narrow shutters whose hinges had been repaired with mismatched metal. The room had a low beam through the center and a scar in the floor where a frame had stood for years. Dust lay thickest along the far wall, but the middle had been swept in an uneven crescent.

Hessa did not step all the way in. She looked at the beam, the shutters, the roof joints and the passage back to the stair.

"Where does the rain go?" she asked.

"Off the outside eave," Ina answered. "When the wind drives it from the other side, that shutter leaks."

"Where do we cook?"

"Not here. Fara can tell you what hot food costs, or the yard can make space for a hearth outside if someone who understands fires approves it. No fire in this room."

"Where is the clean water?"

"I can give you covered jars from a supply I have kept separate. I cannot certify the lane water, and I won't ask you to use it."

The boat-cover maker pressed the wood by the shutter with the back of a knuckle. She let the sound tell her something, then shook her head once.

"This side needs a weather flap," she said. "The wood is sound where the hinge sits, but cloth will take the rain before the gap does."

"Can you make one?" Ina asked.

"Yes. Not for nothing."

"Of course."

Jake smiled before he could help it. A stranger had come into a private workshop, named a defect, and named the cost of addressing it; Ina had not flinched. He had seen enough favors turn into silent resentments to understand the value of a price spoken while both people were still free to refuse.

Orin stood near the wall and held his hands a little apart, measuring a space wider than his shoulders. The two other travelers remained near the stair, watching the baby's face and waiting for Hessa to say whether they might come in.

The apprentice appeared in the doorway below. Jake recognized the clean-cut wooden peg protruding from his pocket. He had made it for the failed trough before Ina told him the old split was too long for a peg to repair.

"That's where the drying racks go," he said.

"Did go," Ina corrected.

"We can build a new trough."

"Not from a peg."

"From boards. We can order them."

"With what? And after we order them, what do we use the yard for while we wait?"

He climbed one step farther. "You told me to keep the frames ready."

"I did. This room is not promised. I am showing it to people who need to see what I am offering."

"The frames are still ours."

"Yes."

"Then whose work is this?"

The question, unlike the peg, did not fit easily in a pocket. Jake saw the apprentice's jaw tighten. The young man had lost an ordinary week in which he would have been paid for an ordinary skill. A roof that might shelter six people could also take away the space where a worker expected to earn his food.

Ina did not ask him to be grateful for a possible new use of the room. She led him to the doorway.

"I can pay you to sort the dry stock for the rest of today," she said quietly enough that Jake could not hear the amount. "After that I cannot promise work I do not have. If we make this room available, you will help decide what is moved and what is kept. You needn't agree to carry a bed."

The apprentice stared at the peg in his hand, then nodded once. He left it on the windowsill and went down.

Hessa watched him disappear.

"We can't take the work of someone who has less choice than we do," she said.

"You aren't taking it," Ina said. "I'm deciding how to use a room I own. That may still hurt him. I won't put the hurt in your name to make myself comfortable."

There it was: an offer with its shadow left visible. Jake had made more generous-sounding promises in his life, and fewer that he could have trusted.

Hessa walked to the center of the floor and set the child down upon her folded canvas. The infant began exploring the seam with both hands. The boards held their weight without complaint. Hessa did not call the room a home.

"What would you ask of us?" she said.

Ina drew a slow breath.

"Let's go where we can all sit. There are six of you, not one voice. There are also people whose work changes if you stay."

### III. The thing they would have to give up

The six travelers gathered beside their cart while Fara cleared the last of the breakfast bowls. The donkey stood tethered in the shade of a wall, its coat brushed clean by the stable keeper. It turned one ear toward them when Hessa approached, then resumed the patient business of looking at its own feed.

The cart had carried the company through smoke and uncertainty. Before the eight departed, it had been one of two vehicles and an argument about which road was less dangerous. Now it seemed too small even for the remaining bundles. One wheel showed a band of newer wood beneath the iron. A corner of the cover had been repaired with thread unlike the rest. The boat-cover maker stood beside that patch and smoothed it once with her palm.

"We can keep the cart as it is," she said. "If the room fails us, we go."

"And if we stay?" Hessa asked.

"Then we have a cart sitting in a yard while we sleep on the boards it could have carried. The room needs shutters covered and places to lie above the floor. We don't have that timber unless somebody sells it to us."

"Could we use the cart sides?"

"We could. It would not be a cart for the road afterward, not without making new sides."

Orin put a hand on the nearest board. "Can the wheels be kept?"

"The axle and wheels can be kept," she said. "They are worth more whole than cut apart."

The infant made a small impatient sound. Hessa took the child onto her hip but let the conversation continue without translating it into a story about the baby's future. Nobody here knew where a child would sleep at the next turning. The question was how the six would survive the next stretch of weather.

One of the unnamed travelers had been holding a narrow wooden case since breakfast. She opened it now. Inside lay a bundle of sewing needles, one bright buckle and a little spool of dark thread. She lifted the buckle from the case.

"I can give this for the cloth," she said to the maker.

"You may need it."

"I have another fastening. Not as good. This is what I can offer."

The maker examined the buckle. "That is a fair price for the shutter flap and one repair to your bag. It isn't enough for all the beds."

"It wasn't meant to be."

Jake had the sudden shame of someone who has watched strangers turn their last belongings into actual measurements while he was waiting for a grand phrase about generosity. He had offered to carry the cart once, when carrying was the only help he knew how to give. This was not a cart to be lifted; it was an object full of possible futures, and no one could move it without ending some of them.

Hessa called each traveler by gesture or name. Orin answered first: he would stay for the proposed term if the room were dry, and wanted the wheels preserved. The maker said she could take the cover down but would require payment for the sewing and for any cloth of her own that she used. The two others considered the roof, the uncertain water and the length of time they could live without moving. The baby answered by rubbing its face into Hessa's collar.

Hessa did not count silence as consent. She returned to the one person who had not answered.

"You don't have to give up the road," she told the maker.

"I'm not giving it up," the woman replied. "I'm putting it where I can find it again."

They unfastened the first sideboard. It took longer than Jake expected. The pins were fitted tight and a corner had swollen after weeks of wet weather. The maker directed the work, choosing which pieces must stay intact and which could be removed without breaking the axle frame. The apprentice, who had come down from the shop, brought a wooden mallet, set it beside her, and did not presume to strike.

Jake asked where to stand.

"On the far side," the maker said. "Hold the board when it comes free. Don't pull against the pin."

He stood where she told him. When the last pin moved, the plank grew suddenly heavy in his arms. It had looked like an ordinary wall while attached to the cart; in his hands it was the length of several days' walking. He felt the grain through his sleeve and watched a line of clean wood appear where the join had protected it from rain.

The cart remained on its wheels. But one side was open now. A person could no longer load the bundles in the old way and simply depart.

At the yard gate, a neighbor stopped to watch.

"What are you doing to that?" the man asked.

"Taking off the sides," Jake answered.

"I can see that."

Hessa came around the wheel. "We're deciding whether to take a room."

"In Ina's shop?"

"If she agrees."

The man shook his head. "Then first her yard, then the passage, then the whole lane. We'll be living inside somebody else's trouble before the water clears."

Hessa did not argue with his fear. She did not thank him for it either.

"You're standing in the gate," she said. "Will you move so we can carry this through?"

He moved, but only because he did not wish to be pushed. Jake could feel the conversation following them as they bore the plank across the stained stones.

### IV. A room with witnesses

Fara insisted that the terms be spoken where all six could hear them.

They stood in the eating room with the door open to the courtyard. The clean water vessels were on the kitchen side, covered and separate from any pail used to carry wash from the street. Ina had brought a piece of charcoal and a scrap of dry board. Hessa put the infant beside her, within reach of the woman's arm, and asked Orin to listen particularly for anything that might bind them beyond the stated nights.

"Twenty-one nights," Ina said. "No promise afterward. If the workroom must reopen, I tell you early enough to move what you've built. If the roof proves unsound, you leave it; I won't take a price for a room that cannot be occupied."

"And the cart?" asked the maker.

"Still yours. You use its boards only if all of you wish it. I'll store the wheels and axle in the dry end of my yard, with a mark on them so nobody mistakes them for mine."

"Water?" Hessa asked.

"Covered jars from a separate supply. Not from the blue street. I will provide the first two. After that we agree on carrying and cost. I am not promising that the wider water is safe."

"Food?"

"Yours to find or purchase," Fara said. "I will tell you what meals cost before I cook them. No one will call an empty plate a debt you accepted without knowing."

Jake had heard Fara give versions of that answer before. She could feed a stranger and still refuse to turn her table into an invisible obligation. He wished he had learned that distinction before filling so many rooms with his own offers.

The apprentice had come in with the others but remained beside the door. Ina turned toward him.

"The racks can be moved to the lower dry corner," she said. "I won't dispose of them. If I have a cloth order I can do without the trough, the frames stay available."

"Not in that room," he said.

"Not while the six are there."

"You make the promise to them and then I'll lose the order."

"If I receive such an order we will make another arrangement or decline it. I won't take work on the strength of a room already offered."

The apprentice's face changed at that. Jake could not tell whether it was anger or the discovery that a decision had finally been spoken in words he could oppose. He walked out to the yard without bowing or offering assent.

Hessa looked after him. "He can refuse to help us."

"He can," Ina said.

The neighbor from the gate appeared at the courtyard entrance with another man behind him. Neither came inside. The first had his arms crossed over a gray vest. He looked past the travelers toward Fara, as though the innkeeper might still be the person who could reverse the affair.

"You have all the good jars," he said. "Then you put six strangers above the dye yard and expect the rest of us to find water somewhere else."

"I have brought two jars from a separate store," Ina answered. "I haven't taken your supply."

"You don't know where the blue went."

"No."

"Then who can say your room is fit for sleeping?"

"No one who hasn't inspected it. We have looked at the floor and roof. We will look again when the weather turns. If something is unsafe, we won't use it."

"You've already taken the cart apart."

"One side," the maker said. "I took it apart."

The second man glanced at the baby, and Jake saw the gesture that would have changed a difficult conversation into an easy performance. Someone would ask whether these people had hearts; someone else would ask who paid for them; everyone would leave feeling either virtuous or cheated. The terms would vanish beneath the spectacle.

Hessa spoke before anybody could make the child an argument.

"We have come to stay for twenty-one nights if Ina keeps the offer," she said. "We are not asking you to call us kin. We won't pretend the water is clean. We can do work that someone wants done, at a price named before it starts. If this room costs another worker his living, we want to hear him say it. We are here to be seen and to be held to the bargain, not to be turned into a story told at a gate."

The room stayed quiet. The neighbor lowered his arms, not in agreement but in the inconvenience of being addressed as a person rather than an audience.

"What happens on the twenty-second night?" he asked.

"I don't know," Hessa said.

It was the first answer that seemed to reach him. He had wanted a certainty to condemn or a promise to collect. She had given him neither.

Ina put the charcoal on the table. "I can promise this room for the twenty-one. I can promise nothing about the town beyond it."

"Then say that on your board," Hessa replied.

They did. Fara read the words aloud twice, slowly, once for those standing at the table and again for the two men outside. The board recorded an arrangement between specific people concerning a specific room. It did not declare a new law, create a public office, settle any claim about water, or tell the six who they must become.

Jake had been watching hands. Ina's stained thumb held the board firm. Hessa pointed when a phrase seemed too broad. The maker put her small buckle down as the first part of her own bargain for work. The apprentice did not return to witness it. Each absence mattered differently from the signatures and marks on the wood.

When it was done, Fara covered the board with a cloth against the damp and said that somebody would have to carry it uphill. She did not volunteer anybody.

Jake asked whether they wanted him to take it.

Hessa looked at him. "Yes. Carry it. Not the decision."

### V. The part of the cart that stayed

By afternoon the sky had cleared enough to throw hard squares of light across the upper room. The workshop below was quiet. There was no hiss from the dye trough, no clatter of cloth beaten against the boards, and no familiar sound of Ina telling the apprentice to keep a hand away from a hot vessel. The silence did not make the shop harmless. The failed trough remained where it had broken, and the stained ground beyond the gate still showed where the water had gone.

The maker hung a weather flap at the leaking shutter. She did not stitch it permanently to the building; she worked loops through existing holes and fastened them with knots that could be undone. The buckle paid for the work lay in her leather roll. Jake saw her check it once and put it away, an object already given a new history.

Orin and the two other travelers carried bundles upstairs. They set them against the dry wall. The sleeping frames were made from cart sideboards laid across surviving shop supports, but the maker left each one low enough to be inspected. She would not let Jake call the first arrangement a bed.

"It's a frame," she said. "It will be a bed when somebody can sleep on it without going through."

He knelt and tested a join. The wood shifted beneath his hand. He stopped.

"Then we need another support."

"We need to know whose support it is before we borrow it."

The apprentice stood by the doorway holding two lengths of sound timber.

"These were meant for a rack," he said. "Ina told me to put them in the dry corner. She says I can offer them for this work if I want to."

"What would you want?" the maker asked.

"Help moving the old frames tomorrow. Two of you, not all six. And I keep the fastening nails when you take this room down."

She inspected the timber. "For two of us, two hours, not all day. The nails can go back to you if they come out sound. If they break, they break."

The apprentice considered. Jake watched his shoulders ease a fraction.

"Two hours," he said.

No one called him generous. They carried the wood upstairs together, each aware of what the other expected. Jake stood aside while the maker and apprentice decided where the supports would go. He was more useful holding a board steady than offering an answer.

The child slept through the hammering on a folded blanket near the far wall. Hessa remained beside the sleeping place until the noise ceased, then began sorting their possessions by what could stay out of the wet and what might be needed quickly on a road. She did not unpack the bundle containing her sister's small slate. That stayed beside the door, within reach, as though news might arrive before dark.

From the upper window Jake could see the second cart below. It stood on two wheels with an exposed bed, one side gone and its surviving board scarred where a pin had come out. He corrected the count in his own head before saying anything. The donkey had been led back to the stable keeper; no animal had been made an ornament to their decision.

The sight hurt in a way he had not anticipated. A cart with no side could be repaired. A room made from its boards could be dismantled. Nothing here was impossible to undo. Yet undoing it would require labor, time, negotiations and weather that no one could promise. He had often mistaken the possibility of reversing a decision for freedom from its cost. Hessa's six had no such luxury. They were choosing between two expenses and paying one in advance.

Eren arrived near the end of the afternoon carrying the stained experimental board from the runoff. Its painted surface was ruined where it had lain in the blue water. The chalk marks on the street were fading, but the board held a tide line too deep to scrub out.

She stopped at the upper stair and looked at the room.

"Do you want this taken away?" she asked Hessa.

"Whose is it?"

"Mine."

"Then why bring it?"

"Because I was going to throw it into the yard and couldn't decide. Ina says you are using scraps to give the room a floor. It might serve as a shelf, if you don't mind the color."

Hessa examined the board without touching the stained face.

"Not where we eat. Not until we know what was in the wash."

"No," Eren said. "I had not thought of that."

They placed it outside, under cover, for a use not yet chosen. Eren neither redeemed her failed picture nor donated a dangerous object for the sake of a beautiful gesture. She accepted the refusal and stayed to watch the maker stitch the last loop at the shutter.

There was no argument about who owned the room when evening came. That had been settled for twenty-one nights and no longer. There was instead the harder question of who could continue to work beneath people who were finally resting overhead.

Ina came to the stair with her apron in her hands. She looked at the suspended racks, the dry stock and the doorway above her.

"Tomorrow," she told the apprentice, "we sort what I can still sell without a wet trough. The day after we find out what timber a replacement would require. I am not promising a reopening date."

He said something Jake could not hear. Ina listened until he finished. Then they walked toward the lower store together.

The building would be different from now on. Not because six people had been declared permanent members of a town. Nobody had the right to make that declaration from one room. It was different because Ina had placed their safety among her working obligations and had made the cost visible to the people it might fall upon. The empty space had entered an argument that would outlive the evening.

### VI. A light where cloth had hung

Fara set out six bowls at supper, and a smaller cup beside Hessa's place. She gave the maker the price of the meal before anyone ate. The woman counted her remaining coins and chose bread and broth; Orin took a smaller portion and put half of his bread beside the old man's bundle. Jake could not tell whether he was sharing with the traveler or saving it for a later hour. He did not ask.

The table was quieter than it had been when the travelers first came through the ash. They had learned where the spoons were kept and how Fara expected the benches returned at the end of the meal. The familiar motions did not grant them a claim on the room, but they made departure from it unexpectedly difficult. A person could become accustomed to a door before it was his to close.

Fara's shortened awning was only a dark cut above the courtyard now. The flowered panel was gone with the eight who had departed. Its absence let Jake see a strip of early evening sky he had never noticed from the bench. He wondered how long it would be before he stopped looking for the old shade. Perhaps the people who returned after winter would not know the space had ever been covered.

He offered to carry one of the clean water jars up to Ina's dry room.

"Ask Hessa how much they can store," Fara said. "Two jars are not a proof of water beyond the lane."

Hessa accepted one jar, saying the second should remain covered below until there was a secure place for it. The maker had repaired the shutter but had not finished a stand for the vessel. Jake carried the first jar with both arms, taking the stairs slowly.

At the top, the room smelled of old cloth, worked timber and the faint dry dust of a place disturbed after a long stillness. The sleeping frames cast broad shadows across the floor. The baby had been laid down on a blanket. The others were settling bags and tools where they would be able to find them in darkness. Nobody had put a name on the door.

Hessa met him beside the beam.

"Here," she said, showing him a cleared patch well away from the sleeping places. "We'll need a cover that stays on."

He set down the jar. Its weight left a tingling in his forearms. He had carried heavier things for pay and lighter things to prove himself indispensable. This one was a task with an end: water in an agreed place. He did not need to tell Hessa what the room meant.

"Will you look for your sister from here?" he asked.

She studied the low shutters. "I will ask for news where news can come. I won't make the others walk every road because I have only one name to follow."

"I could ask at the stoneworks."

"You can ask, if you go. Don't say you found her until you've found her."

"I wouldn't."

Hessa looked at him steadily. He understood that she was not accusing him of a particular lie. She was setting a term more difficult than his good intentions: a person waiting for news had to be able to trust the shape of its uncertainty.

"I'll tell you only what I know," he said.

"That will be enough."

Jake went down while the light was leaving the stair. Through the open lower door he saw Ina tying a cord around the dry stock, the apprentice beside her, the two figures bent toward work that still belonged to the shop. A small lamp had been set upstairs at a safe distance from the canvas and loose timber; Hessa made the maker shift it farther from the shutter. Jake heard the correction and the quiet answer to it. The room was being governed by the people in it.

Outside, the street retained a blue darkness in the joints of its stones. The covered jars at Fara's remained separate. No one had proved the unknown water fit for drinking, and nobody had found the distant fire. The eight travelers who had taken the first cart remained beyond the settlement's knowledge. Pell and Mael were still somewhere among the living with explanations unfinished. Esi had not answered the letter Jake had sent. None of those facts had been improved by the light now burning over Ina's workshop.

But from the lane the light could be seen through the upper shutter. It shone where cloth had once hung, and an observer who did not know the bargain might mistake it for a sign that the whole building had changed hands.

A carter stopped Jake near the bend. He wore a travel cloak with one shoulder damp and carried a short pole across his back. Jake did not recognize him.

"Is there lodging above the dye place?" the man asked.

"For six people," Jake said. "For a fixed number of nights."

"Only six?"

"That is the offer they made."

The man looked toward the shutter. "I heard the room was open."

Jake considered how quickly a statement could travel after leaving the mouth that had made it. He remembered the singer's name printed without her permission, the false summons sent along a road, the colored water that found ways through walls no one had examined. A room offered to six people could become a rumor of a refuge large enough for everybody. The rumor would arrive before the lumber, the water and the wages required to make it true.

"Who told you?" he asked.

The carter moved the pole from one shoulder to the other. "A man by the lower turn. Said the dye woman had opened her house."

Jake looked again at the light. He did not know whether the traveler had a place to sleep or whether Fara could offer him one; he would not declare the upper room public property by repeating a stranger's words.

"Speak to Ina," he said. "The room is hers. Don't tell the next man it's his until she's heard him."

The carter hesitated, then walked toward the yard gate. Jake followed at a distance sufficient to let the traveler speak for himself. The blue marks were under their feet. Above them the new lamp held steady, and below the shutter Ina opened the door to hear what the man wanted.

The road, which had brought six people to a room, was already bringing another question to it.
